items.title: Home
items.text:
A wend expression records how a path is built — which parts are literal, which are parameters, how values are formatted — instead of collapsing it to a string. The same expression can be resolved, partially bound, transformed structurally, matched against concrete paths, used to discover files on disk, compiled for batch resolution, and inferred from an existing directory tree.

from wend import Param, Segment, T

root = Param("root")
split = Segment("split", choices={"train", "test"})
idx = Param("idx", type=int)

shard = root / split / T(t"chunk_{idx:04d}.parquet")

>>> shard
PathExpr('{root}/{split}/chunk_{idx:04d}.parquet')
>>> shard.render(root="data", split="train", idx=7)
'data/train/chunk_0007.parquet'
>>> shard.match("data/test/chunk_0042.parquet")
Match('data/test/chunk_0042.parquet', {'root': 'data', 'split': 'test', 'idx': 42})
>>> [(m["split"], m["idx"]) for m in shard.glob(root="data")]
[('test', 0), ('train', 0), ('train', 1), ('train', 3)]
  • render substitutes the values and applies the formatting: idx=7 becomes 0007.
  • match goes the other way and returns typed values: idx is the integer 42. It returns None for a path the expression does not describe, such as data/val/chunk_0001.parquet (val is not a declared split) or data/test/chunk_42.parquet (not four digits).
  • glob lists only the directories the expression can reach, and yields the same Match objects for the files it finds.
>>> print(shard.match("data/val/chunk_0001.parquet"))
None
>>> print(shard.match("data/test/chunk_42.parquet"))
None

items.title: Install
items.text:
wend needs Python 3.14 or later.

pip install wend

The optional integrations are extras: wend[pydantic] for path fields on Pydantic models, wend[fsspec] for object stores, and wend[polars] for resolving whole columns of a DataFrame.

wend grew out of the Future Paths essays, which set out what Python paths could keep track of beyond a concrete value.

items.title: Future Paths and wend
items.text:
wend grew out of Future Paths, five essays written in January 2026 on what Python paths could keep track of beyond a concrete value. This page maps each essay to the library as it is now. Using wend does not require reading them.

The essays share one distinction, stated in the first: describing a path is different from realising it as a concrete value. Most of what they propose, and most of what wend does, follows from keeping the description.

items.title: Part 1: Semantic types
items.text:
The essay asks for paths that carry what the programmer means by them: that a path must exist or must not, is a file or a directory, is a fragment to be placed under a root, or must stay inside a directory. It then sketches lenses, lineage, content addressing, directory schemas, schema inference, an algebra of path sets, late binding and virtual filesystems.

Its fragment and late-binding sketches work as written, with wend's names:

>>> from wend import P, Param
>>> leaf = P("bar")
>>> [p.render() for p in map(leaf.under, ["foo1", "foo2"])]
['foo1/bar', 'foo2/bar']
>>> ROOT = Param("root")
>>> CONFIG = ROOT / "config.yaml"
>>> CONFIG.resolve(root="/actual/root")
PosixPath('/actual/root/config.yaml')
the essay's sketch in wend Path.fragment(...), leaf.under(parent) an expression and under PathVar("root"), CONFIG.collect(paths) Param, resolve, and bindings from objects FilePath, DirectoryPath, NewPath the conditions File, Dir, Exists and Absent Path[Readable], Path[Writable, MayCreate] Readable, Writable, Creatable and Listable Path[Under[STATIC_ROOT]] Under, and segment parameters, which cannot traverse pre- and postconditions on pipeline steps requires, ensures and Step PathLens(forward=..., backward=...) Lens, built from two expressions instead of two functions .tag(...), provenance, trace_lineage() tag, explain and Ledger content-addressed paths, as in Nix content_key @directory_schema class MLProject wend.schema.Tree, with validate and scaffold schema inference, after genson wend.infer.infer and from_inferred a union of UserConfig, SystemConfig and DefaultConfig, tried in order; &, - and PathQ unions with first, and queries XDG.CACHE_HOME wend.anchors fsspec and other filesystems wend.fs.FsspecFS, for glob and infer

What changed on the way.

  • The capabilities are runtime checks, not types. Path[Readable] in a signature is something a type checker could verify. wend's conditions are declared on an expression and checked by check and Step when the program runs; a type checker sees a PathExpr. The conditions journal entry records what static checking could add.
  • The lens is derived, not written. The essay's lens takes a forward and a backward function. wend's takes two expressions, and derives both directions by matching one and rendering the other, so the two directions cannot disagree.
  • The schema is a class of entries, with cardinality per directory and a report of every difference at once, rather than typed attribute access alone.

items.title: Part 2: Connectivity
items.text:
The essay observes that after config = project_root / "config.yaml", the fact that config was built from project_root is gone. It asks for a relation type, base tracking, rebasing, sibling and cousin relations, composition rules, and some integration with types.

All but the last are in wend (Relations):

>>> Root = Param("Root")
>>> csv_in = Root / "data" / "input.csv"
>>> schema = csv_in.sibling("schema.json")
>>> schema.render(Root="/tmp/proj")
'/tmp/proj/data/schema.json'
>>> moved = schema.rebase(csv_in, P("/archive/input.csv"))
>>> moved.render()
'/archive/schema.json'

Composition preserves the chain: a path derived from a derived path keeps both steps, so rebasing any path in the chain moves everything derived from it. Type-level connectivity (config: Path[Under[root]]) needs dependent types, which Python does not have; Under is checked at runtime instead, lexically by render and with symlinks resolved by check.

items.title: Part 3: Deferred path-ification
items.text:
The essay builds a proof of concept on Python 3.14's t-strings: parameters stay symbolic inside a template, joins build a tree, and resolve substitutes values, with parent, with_suffix and with_name working before any value is known. wend keeps all of it, and the essay's examples run as written:

>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> from wend import T
>>> root, idx, total = Param("root"), Param("idx"), Param("total")
>>> chunk_file_t = root / "chunks" / T(t"chunk_{idx:03}-of-{total:03}.parquet")
>>> chunk_file_t.resolve({"root": Path("/data"), "idx": 1, "total": 10})
PosixPath('/data/chunks/chunk_001-of-010.parquet')
>>> chunk_file_t.parent.resolve({"root": Path("/data")})
PosixPath('/data/chunks')
>>> chunk_file_t.with_suffix(".json").resolve(
...     {"root": Path("/data"), "idx": 5, "total": 10}
... )
PosixPath('/data/chunks/chunk_005-of-010.json')

What changed is the structure underneath. The proof of concept was a tree of join nodes. wend keeps every expression in a normal form, a head followed by segments, so the number of segments is known before binding. That one change is what makes the rest sound:

  • an operation is computed from the structure only when the structure decides it, and is deferred to pathlib otherwise (Operations);
  • a value bound to a segment parameter cannot add segments, so it cannot traverse (Parameters);
  • an expression can be matched back against a path (Rendering and matching). None of the essays has matching; it came with the normal form.

items.title: Part 4: Compilation theory
items.text:
The essay frames path expressions as term rewriting, with three rules: parent–join cancellation, constant folding and suffix-chain collapse. It then sketches a register machine for executing them, and concludes that Python, not a parser, should build the expression tree.

The conclusion holds: the expression tree is built by Python's own operators. The three rules hold too, with the condition the essay did not state. Parent–join cancellation is valid only when the right operand is exactly one segment, so wend applies it only then:

>>> from wend import SubPath
>>> (Root / "a/b").parent
PathExpr('{Root}/a')
>>> (Root / SubPath("rel")).parent
PathExpr('parent({Root}/{rel...})')

wend 0.1 applied the rule by the type of a node rather than its number of segments, and gave /x for (root / "a/b").parent where pathlib gives /x/a. The retrospective records this. The current rules are not a rewrite system applied afterwards: they are what the normal form computes when an expression is built, and the contract states the result they must agree with, which the tests check against an eager pathlib oracle.

The register machine was not built. Its main benefit, computing a shared sub-path once, appears as compile_many, which looks up, checks and formats each parameter once for a whole set of expressions.

items.title: Part 5: Lazy execution
items.text:
The essay describes a Rust implementation behind pyo3: an arena of nodes, an optimiser, and a slot-based executor, with compile_path(expr).resolve(...) from Python.

wend has no Rust backend. Its goal, compiling once and resolving many times without walking the tree, is met in Python:

  • compile generates a specialised Python function per expression, with validation and formatting inlined;
  • compile().many and compile().columns render in bulk;
  • wend.frame.resolve_frame renders whole Polars columns.

The essay's API also differs: its T("chunk_{idx}.parquet", ["idx"]) took formatting out of the template and had the caller format each value, which wend's t-string templates keep in place. Whether a native backend is worth building is open, to be decided on measurements: issue #37 tracks it, and the journal records what a backend would need to beat.

items.title: What is still open
items.text:
• Static checking. Capabilities, containment and connectivity as types that a type checker verifies, rather than conditions checked at runtime.
  • A native backend, only where measurements justify one (#37).
  • Effects as data. Parts 2 and 5 suggest reporting every filesystem effect a program can have. Step.effects() lists what each path of a step declares, but nothing collects them across a program.

Project history lists the journal entries that record how each part was built, including the trajectory entry, which tells the same story in more detail.

items.title: Project history
items.text:
wend's design decisions are recorded in a development journal: dated Markdown files in docs/journal/ of the repository. Each entry covers one piece of work and records what was built, the decisions behind it and what was measured, so that the next change starts from the reasons. The format is described in docs/JOURNAL.md.

Claims in an entry carry a label:

  • [Fact]: checked against a primary source: the code, a test, an essay or a benchmark;
  • [Measured]: a number from a stated measurement;
  • [Interpretation]: a reading of the facts;
  • [Proposal]: a direction offered for decision;
  • [Decision]: what was chosen, and why.

items.title: How wend works
items.text:
pathlib composes a path from its parts, and the result is a concrete value:

>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> split, i = "train", 7
>>> Path("data") / split / f"chunk_{i:04d}.parquet"
PosixPath('data/train/chunk_0007.parquet')

split and i have been substituted and the 04d format has been applied, and the value records neither the parameters nor the format. Code that needs the layout again, to read split and i back out of a filename, to list the chunks that exist or to check that one is present, has to state it again, for example as a regular expression or a glob pattern.

A wend expression is the description of the path:

from wend import Param, T

root, split, idx = Param("root"), Param("split"), Param("idx", type=int)
shard = root / split / T(t"chunk_{idx:04d}.parquet")

>>> shard
PathExpr('{root}/{split}/chunk_{idx:04d}.parquet')
>>> shard.render(root="data", split="train", idx=7)
'data/train/chunk_0007.parquet'
>>> shard.match("data/train/chunk_0007.parquet")
Match('data/train/chunk_0007.parquet', {'root': 'data', 'split': 'train', 'idx': 7})

It keeps its parameters (with their kinds, types and choices), its literal parts, its formatting and the operations applied to it. It becomes a concrete path only when it is rendered. For every set of values it accepts, the rendered path is the path pathlib computes from the same values. Everything else wend does is done with the description.

items.title: The concept pages
items.text:
Together with the Quickstart, this page is enough to use the library. The other pages explain one part each, and can be read in any order.

  • Expressions: what an expression records, and how P, T and / build one from text, parameters and t-strings.
  • Parameters: the four kinds of parameter, type=, choices= and default=, and why a value bound to a segment parameter cannot leave its directory.
  • Operations: which path operations are computed from structure, which wait for values, and which are rejected.
  • Rendering and matching: the two directions, how matches are verified, and why an ambiguous path is an error.
  • Relations: how an expression remembers the paths it was built from, and how rebasing one path moves the paths derived from it.
  • Effects: which operations touch the filesystem, and how conditions declare what a path must be.

The precise rules are in SEMANTICS.md, the contract that the tests check wend against.

items.title: Effects
items.text:
from wend import Absent, Creatable, Exists, File, P, Param, Readable, T

root, day = Param("root"), Param("day")

src = (P(root) / "raw" / T(t"{day}.csv")).requires(File, Exists, Readable)
dst = (P(root) / "clean" / T(t"{day}.csv")).requires(Absent, Creatable)
dst = dst.ensures(File, Exists)

The directory data/raw/ holds one file, mon.csv:

>>> src.render(root="data", day="tue")
'data/raw/tue.csv'
>>> src.check(root="data", day="tue")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.MissingPathError: 'data/raw/tue.csv' does not exist (required: Exists)
>>> src.check(root="data", day="mon")
PosixPath('data/raw/mon.csv')

src declares that its path must be an existing, readable file when it is used. render returns the path for tue although no such file exists, because it reads nothing from the filesystem. check renders the path, tests each condition against the filesystem, and raises for the first one that fails.

items.title: Pure operations and effects
items.text:
Building an expression, every path operation, bind, render, resolve, match, match_all, the relations and compile are pure. Their results depend only on the expression and the bindings.

These operations touch the filesystem:

  • glob lists directories to find the paths an expression describes.
  • check and confirm test an expression's conditions, and a Step tests those of several paths.
  • PathUnion.first returns the first alternative of a union whose path exists and meets its own conditions.
  • Tree.validate reads a directory tree and reports where it differs from a schema. Tree.scaffold creates the schema's directories, and empty files with files=True. It never overwrites a path.
  • Ledger records which files were made from which, with digests of their contents, and reads the files again to say what is stale.
from wend import Dir
from wend.schema import Tree


class Project(Tree):
    data = Dir("data")
    config = File("config.yaml")

>>> project = Project("project")
>>> project.scaffold()
[PosixPath('project'), PosixPath('project/data')]
>>> project.validate()
Report('project': 1 missing)
  <missing 'project/config.yaml' [config]>

items.title: Conditions
items.text:
requires declares preconditions, which must hold before a path is used. ensures declares postconditions, which must hold after it has been produced. check tests the first and confirm the second.

condition holds when Exists the path exists (symlinks followed) Absent nothing is at the path, not even a broken symlink File / Dir the path is missing, or is a regular file / a directory Readable the path exists and can be read Listable the path is a directory that can be listed Writable the path exists and can be written, or is Creatable Creatable the path exists, or its nearest existing ancestor is a directory that entries can be created in Under(base) the path is lexically inside base, and resolving symlinks keeps it there

Conditions are not part of the path. An expression with conditions equals the same expression without them:

>>> src == P(root) / "raw" / T(t"{day}.csv")
True
>>> dst
PathExpr('{root}/clean/{day}.csv', requires=(Absent, Creatable), ensures=(File, Exists))

Conditions that cannot hold together in one phase, such as Exists and Absent, raise PathOperationError when they are declared.

items.title: Conditions that need no filesystem
items.text:
Two conditions are enforced from the expression and its bindings alone.

render checks Under(base) lexically: a binding cannot lead outside the base through .. or an absolute value. check also resolves symlinks.

>>> from wend import AnyPath, Under
>>> upload = (P(root) / AnyPath("rel")).requires(Under(P(root)))
>>> upload.render(root="/srv", rel="a/b.txt")
'/srv/a/b.txt'
>>> upload.render(root="/srv", rel="../etc/passwd")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.ContainmentError: '/srv/../etc/passwd' is not under '/srv' (required: Under('{root}'))

File is a fact about the structure: nothing can be joined below a path declared to be a file, so the join raises when the expression is built.

>>> src / "x"
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.PathOperationError: '{root}/raw/{day}.csv' is declared a File: nothing can be joined below it

items.title: Steps
items.text:
A Step groups the paths that one step of a pipeline uses. Its bindings are shared, and each path takes the parameters it uses.

>>> from wend import Step
>>> convert = Step(src=src, dst=dst)
>>> convert.effects()
[<src: read {root}/raw/{day}.csv>, <dst: create {root}/clean/{day}.csv>]
>>> with convert(root="data", day="mon") as p:
...     p["dst"].parent.mkdir()
...     _ = p["dst"].write_text(p["src"].read_text().upper())
>>> Path("data/clean/mon.csv").read_text()
'A,B\n1,2\n'

Entering the with block checks every precondition and gives the rendered paths. Leaving it without an exception checks every postcondition, here that dst now exists as a file. A second run fails before its body runs, because dst must be absent:

>>> with convert(root="data", day="mon") as p:
...     print("not reached")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.PathExistsError: 'data/clean/mon.csv' already exists (required: Absent)

effects lists what each path declares it is used for: read, write, create, list or delete. It reports the declarations, and does not observe what the step does.

items.title: Errors
items.text:
Each failed condition raises a ConditionError. Its path is the rendered path and its condition is the condition that failed. Each subclass also derives from the builtin exception for the same failure, so existing handlers keep working. InvalidBindingError is a ValueError.

error also a raised when MissingPathError FileNotFoundError a path that must exist does not PathExistsError FileExistsError a path that must be absent exists CapabilityError PermissionError a path cannot be read, written, created or listed WrongKindError a path is not the declared kind: a file, or a directory ContainmentError InvalidBindingError a path is not under its declared base NoAlternativeError FileNotFoundError no alternative of a union qualifies for first 
>>> try:
...     src.check(root="data", day="tue")
... except FileNotFoundError as e:
...     print(type(e).__name__, e.path)
MissingPathError data/raw/tue.csv

items.title: Checks are point-in-time
items.text:
A check describes the filesystem at the moment it runs. A path that exists when it is checked may be gone when it is opened, and a symlink may be replaced between the two. Checks are not atomic with any later use of the path, and Readable, Writable and the other capabilities report the permissions of the real user. Conditions state what a program expects and catch mistakes. They are not a sandbox, and neither is glob's symlink policy.

Conditions are checked when the program runs. A type checker sees a PathExpr, with no conditions in its type.

items.title: Other filesystems
items.text: glob and infer read a tree through a wend.fs.FileSystem: the local disk by default, or the filesystem given with fs=. With the fsspec extra, url_to_fs gives an FsspecFS for an object store and the path within it. check, confirm, Step, first, Tree.validate, Tree.scaffold and Ledger use the local filesystem.

items.title: Expressions
items.text:
from wend import P, Param, T

root, split = Param("root"), Param("split")
idx = Param("idx", type=int)

joined = root / "data" / split / T(t"chunk_{idx:04d}.parquet")
written = T(t"{root}/data/{split}/chunk_{idx:04d}.parquet")

>>> joined
PathExpr('{root}/data/{split}/chunk_{idx:04d}.parquet')
>>> joined == written
True
>>> joined.params
{'root': Param('root'), 'split': Param('split'), 'idx': Param('idx', type=int)}

The two expressions are built differently and describe the same path, so they are equal. Each one records the structure of the path, and params lists its parameters with their declarations.

items.title: Describing and realising a path
items.text:
pathlib composes paths well. Its result is a concrete value:

>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> Path("data") / "train" / f"chunk_{7:04d}.parquet"
PosixPath('data/train/chunk_0007.parquet')

The f-string is formatted before the join, so the value holds the text chunk_0007. It records neither the 04d format nor which part of the name was a number.

A wend expression is a description of the path. It is realised as a concrete path by render (a str) or resolve (a pathlib.Path), which apply the same pathlib rules to the values given:

>>> joined.resolve(root=".", split="train", idx=7)
PosixPath('data/train/chunk_0007.parquet')

The description itself can also be matched against paths, used to find files, transformed, or bound in part.

items.title: What an expression records
items.text:
• Literal parts: text that is the same in every rendering, such as data, chunk_ and .parquet.
  • Parameters: named parts whose values are given later. Each keeps its declaration: its kind, type, choices and default (Parameters).
  • Formatted fields: interpolations such as {idx:04d}, with their conversion and format spec, applied when the path is rendered.
  • Operations: parent, with_suffix, relative_to and the others, applied to the structure where possible and recorded where not (Operations).

The pattern property, which the repr shows, writes this structure out in t-string syntax.

items.title: Building an expression
items.text:
• P(x) makes an expression from a str, an os.PathLike, a Param, a t-string or another expression.
  • T(t"...") makes an expression from a t-string.
  • / and joinpath join. The right-hand side can be any of the values P takes, and a t-string on the right needs no T:
>>> name = Param("name")
>>> P("data") / t"{name}.csv"
PathExpr('data/{name}.csv')

A str joined with / is a literal path, with pathlib's rules. Its separators make segments, and an absolute path replaces what came before it:

>>> P("data") / "raw/2026"
PathExpr('data/raw/2026')
>>> P("data") / "/srv"
PathExpr('/srv')

An f-string formats a Param into text before wend receives it. wend detects this and raises TypeError:

>>> P(f"{root}/data")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
TypeError: A Param was formatted into a plain string (an f-string or str.format); use a t-string instead, e.g. T(t'chunk_{idx:04d}')

items.title: How a t-string is split
items.text:
A t-string's literal text is split at every /, so the number of segments and their positions are known before any value is bound. This is why operations on the structure need no values:

>>> T(t"reports/{split}/{name}.csv").parent
PathExpr('reports/{split}')

A value bound later adds segments only through a parameter whose kind accepts a path of several segments, such as the parameter at the head or a SubPath. Anywhere else, a / in a value is rejected (Parameters).

items.title: Path operands and formatted fields
items.text:
An interpolation is one of two things, depending on where it stands:

  • A path operand is an interpolation that forms a whole segment, with no conversion and no format spec, such as {root} and {split} in t"{root}/data/{split}". It is joined exactly as / joins it, so T(t"{root}/data") equals root / "data".
  • A formatted field is any other interpolation, such as {idx:04d} in t"chunk_{idx:04d}", {name} in t"{name}.csv" or {name!r}. Its value is formatted as an f-string formats it, and the text becomes part of one segment.

A template renders as formatting the t-string as an f-string and parsing the result would, except where that would change the path's structure. A path operand is joined, so an empty value at the head is the empty path and does not make the path absolute:

>>> value = ""
>>> T(t"{root}/data").render(root=value)
'data'
>>> Path(f"{value}/data")
PosixPath('/data')

The text of a formatted field cannot contain /, since it is part of one segment:

>>> T(t"{name}.csv").render(name="a/b")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.InvalidBindingError: {name} formats 'a/b' to 'a/b', which contains a separator

SEMANTICS.md §4.1 lists every case where a template differs from formatting the t-string as an f-string.

items.title: Dynamic format specs
items.text:
A format spec can contain parameters of its own:

width = Param("width", type=int)
chunk = T(t"chunk_{idx:0{width}d}.parquet")

>>> chunk
PathExpr('chunk_{idx:0{width}d}.parquet')
>>> chunk.render(idx=7, width=6)
'chunk_000007.parquet'

width is a parameter like any other, and is checked against its declaration. A path can be matched once the spec is fixed, by binding width first:

>>> chunk.bind(width=6).match("chunk_000007.parquet")
Match('chunk_000007.parquet', {'idx': 7})

items.title: Rendering and matching
items.text:
from wend import P, Param, T

idx = Param("idx", type=int)
chunk = P("data") / T(t"chunk_{idx:04d}.parquet")

>>> chunk.render(idx=7)
'data/chunk_0007.parquet'
>>> chunk.match("data/chunk_0007.parquet")
Match('data/chunk_0007.parquet', {'idx': 7})
>>> print(chunk.match("data/chunk_007.parquet"))
None

An expression goes in two directions. render takes bindings and returns a path. match takes a path and returns the bindings that render to it, or None when there are none. chunk_007 has no match: {idx:04d} renders 7 as 0007, and renders no integer as 007.

items.title: Rendering
items.text:
• render returns the canonical path as a str.
  • resolve returns the same path as a pathlib.Path, or as the class given with cls=.

Bindings can be keywords, a mapping keyed by name or by Param, or an object whose fields are named after the parameters, such as a dataclass or a Pydantic model (bindings shows what an object binds). Keywords take precedence.

>>> from pathlib import PurePosixPath
>>> chunk.render({idx: 7})
'data/chunk_0007.parquet'
>>> chunk.resolve(idx=7, cls=PurePosixPath)
PurePosixPath('data/chunk_0007.parquet')
>>> chunk.render()
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.MissingBindingError: Missing bindings: ['idx']

A parameter with no binding takes its default if it declares one. Otherwise rendering raises MissingBindingError. A value that its declaration or its position does not accept raises InvalidBindingError (Parameters).

items.title: Matching
items.text:
match returns a Match: a read-only mapping of parameter names to values, with the matched path as .path. The path is normalised as pathlib normalises it before it is matched, so data//chunk_0007.parquet and data/./chunk_0007.parquet match too.

Values are typed. A parameter declared with type= is read as that type. An undeclared one is read as the type its format spec implies: {n:d} and {n:x} read integers, and a field with no spec reads a str.

>>> n, label = Param("n"), Param("label")
>>> T(t"run_{n:x}").match("run_1f")
Match('run_1f', {'n': 31})
>>> T(t"run_{label}").match("run_1f")
Match('run_1f', {'label': '1f'})

items.title: Matches are verified
items.text:
Every candidate reading is rendered again and compared with the path before it is returned, so a match always renders to exactly the path it came from. A format spec's width is a minimum, so a longer number is a valid rendering:

>>> chunk.match("data/chunk_12345.parquet")
Match('data/chunk_12345.parquet', {'idx': 12345})
>>> chunk.render(idx=12345)
'data/chunk_12345.parquet'

glob verifies the paths it finds in the same way.

items.title: Ambiguity is an error
items.text:
Some paths can be read in more than one way. match raises AmbiguousMatchError for them. It does not choose one of the readings.

stem, ext = Param("stem"), Param("ext")
dist = P("dist") / T(t"{stem}.{ext}")

>>> dist.match("dist/tool.whl")
Match('dist/tool.whl', {'stem': 'tool', 'ext': 'whl'})
>>> dist.match("dist/tool-1.0.tar.gz")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.AmbiguousMatchError: 'dist/tool-1.0.tar.gz' matches ambiguously: ...
>>> dist.match_all("dist/tool-1.0.tar.gz")
[{'stem': 'tool-1', 'ext': '0.tar.gz'}, {'stem': 'tool-1.0', 'ext': 'tar.gz'}, {'stem': 'tool-1.0.tar', 'ext': 'gz'}]

match_all lists every verified reading. Each reading renders to the path, so any choice among them would be a guess about which one was meant. The error's candidates attribute holds the same list.

Declaring what a field can hold, or binding a parameter, leaves one reading:

>>> known = Param("ext", choices={"whl", "tar.gz"})
>>> package = P("dist") / T(t"{stem}.{known}")
>>> package.match("dist/tool-1.0.tar.gz")
Match('dist/tool-1.0.tar.gz', {'stem': 'tool-1.0', 'ext': 'tar.gz'})
>>> dist.bind(ext="gz").match("dist/tool-1.0.tar.gz")
Match('dist/tool-1.0.tar.gz', {'stem': 'tool-1.0.tar'})

Other ambiguous shapes are adjacent string fields such as {a}{b}, and a free head parameter followed by a SubPath, where the split between the two is not fixed. By default glob raises AmbiguousMatchError for the first ambiguous path it finds. ambiguous="skip" leaves such paths out, and a callable receives each error (wend.glob).

items.title: Not invertible
items.text:
An expression that starts with a deferred operation, or a field whose text is derived from another path, cannot be read back from a path. match raises NotInvertibleError and names the construct. Binding its parameters first makes the expression invertible:

>>> from wend import SubPath
>>> root, rel = Param("root"), SubPath("rel")
>>> up = (root / rel).parent
>>> up.match("/srv/a")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.NotInvertibleError: 'parent({root}/{rel...})' starts with a deferred 'parent'; bind its parameters before matching
>>> up.bind(root="/srv", rel="a/b").match("/srv/a")
Match('/srv/a', {})

A format spec that depends on an unbound parameter, such as {idx:0{width}d}, raises it too (Expressions).

items.title: Operations
items.text:
from wend import Param, SubPath, T

root, split, rel = Param("root"), Param("split"), SubPath("rel")
idx = Param("idx", type=int)

shard = root / split / T(t"chunk_{idx:04d}.parquet")
source = root / rel

>>> shard.parent
PathExpr('{root}/{split}')
>>> shard.with_suffix(".json")
PathExpr('{root}/{split}/chunk_{idx:04d}.json')
>>> source.parent
PathExpr('parent({root}/{rel...})')

shard's last segment is known from its structure, so its parent and its suffix are computed with no values bound. source ends in a sub-path of zero or more segments, so its parent depends on the value of rel, and the operation waits for it.

Every operation is one of three kinds: static, deferred or rejected.

items.title: Static operations
items.text:
A static operation is computed from the structure, without bindings:

  • parent, name and with_name of an expression whose last part is a segment;
  • stem, suffix and with_suffix, when the last dot of that segment is in literal text, no field after it can contain a dot (an integer field cannot), and a character other than a dot comes before it;
  • relative_to a structural prefix;
  • bind.
>>> shard.name
Text('chunk_{idx:04d}.parquet')
>>> shard.stem
Text('chunk_{idx:04d}')
>>> shard.suffix
Text('.parquet')
>>> shard.with_name("index.json")
PathExpr('{root}/{split}/index.json')
>>> shard.relative_to(root)
PathExpr('{split}/chunk_{idx:04d}.parquet')

name, stem and suffix are strings, so they return a Text: a symbolic string with its own render.

A static operation can remove parameters. shard.parent.parent is {root}: the value of split does not change it, so the result has no split and needs no binding for it.

>>> shard.parent.parent
PathExpr('{root}')
>>> shard.parent.parent.render(root="data")
'data'

items.title: Deferred operations
items.text:
A deferred operation depends on values that are not bound yet. It is recorded in the expression, shown in the pattern as a call, and evaluated with pathlib once its inputs are bound:

>>> source.parent.render(root="/srv", rel="a/b")
'/srv/a'
>>> source.parent.render(root="/srv", rel="")
'/'

With rel="" the path is /srv, so its parent is /, as pathlib computes it.

The suffix of a free-form string field is deferred too, since the value can contain a dot:

>>> name = Param("name")
>>> upload = root / "uploads" / name
>>> upload.suffix
Text('{suffix({root}/uploads/{name})}')
>>> upload.suffix.render(root="data", name="photo.tar.gz")
'.gz'

The suffix of {name}.csv is deferred for a similar reason. With name="" the segment is .csv, a hidden file whose suffix is "":

>>> (root / T(t"{name}.csv")).suffix
Text('{suffix({root}/{name}.csv)}')
>>> (root / T(t"report_{name}.csv")).suffix
Text('.csv')

An expression that starts with a deferred operation cannot be matched against a path until its parameters are bound (Rendering and matching).

items.title: Rejected operations
items.text:
An operation that is invalid for every binding raises PathOperationError when the expression is built. It is a ValueError, as pathlib's error for the same operation is.

>>> from wend import P
>>> P("/").with_name("x")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.PathOperationError: '/' has an empty name
>>> shard.with_suffix("json")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.PathOperationError: Invalid suffix 'json'

items.title: bind is partial evaluation
items.text:
bind substitutes some parameters and folds what becomes static. The others stay free.

>>> shard.bind(root="data")
PathExpr('data/{split}/chunk_{idx:04d}.parquet')
>>> shard.bind(root="data", split="train", idx=3).is_static
True

A value can also be an expression, which places the path under another one, or a Param, which renames:

>>> shard.bind(root=P("/mnt") / Param("user"))
PathExpr('/mnt/{user}/{split}/chunk_{idx:04d}.parquet')
>>> shard.bind(split=Param("part"))
PathExpr('{root}/{part}/chunk_{idx:04d}.parquet')

bind does not apply defaults (Parameters).

items.title: render equals the pathlib computation
items.text:
For every binding that an expression and its sub-expressions accept, render returns the path that the eager pathlib computation of the same operations returns, applied to the formatted strings:

>>> from pathlib import PurePosixPath
>>> meta = shard.with_suffix(".json").relative_to(root)
>>> meta.render(root="data", split="train", idx=3)
'train/chunk_0003.json'
>>> eager = PurePosixPath("data") / "train" / f"chunk_{3:04d}.parquet"
>>> str(eager.with_suffix(".json").relative_to("data"))
'train/chunk_0003.json'

A binding that would make pathlib change the path's structure without an error is rejected with InvalidBindingError:

  • a separator inside a segment;
  • an empty segment, or a . segment;
  • an escaping ..;
  • a value that violates a declared type or choices.

Evaluation is non-strict. A part of an expression that an operation discards, such as the segment parent drops or everything before an absolute join, need not be evaluated, so a value bound only to that part may go unchecked. This is the one case where render can return a path for a binding that the eager computation rejects.

items.title: Parameters
items.text:
from wend import P, Param

asset = P("/srv/static") / Param("name")

>>> asset.render(name="logo.png")
'/srv/static/logo.png'
>>> asset.render(name="../../etc/passwd")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.InvalidBindingError: name='../../etc/passwd' is not a single path segment; declare 'name' with SubPath('name') to bind multi-segment paths

name comes after the head of the expression, so it binds exactly one path segment. ../../etc/passwd is four segments, so the binding is rejected. pathlib joins the same value as written:

>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> Path("/srv/static") / "../../etc/passwd"
PosixPath('/srv/static/../../etc/passwd')

items.title: The four kinds
items.text:
A parameter's kind says what it may bind to when it is used as a path operand:

kind constructor accepts path (default at the head) Param("root"), AnyPath(...) any path; pathlib join semantics absolute Absolute(...) an absolute path segment (default after the head) Param(...), Segment(...) exactly one segment: no /, not "", . or .. sub-path SubPath(...) a relative path of zero or more segments, without ..

A Param takes its kind from its position. At the head of an expression, with nothing before it, it is a path. Anywhere else it is a segment. The other constructors fix the kind wherever the parameter is used: AnyPath, Absolute, Segment and SubPath.

from wend import Absolute, Segment, SubPath, T

root, rel, stem = Param("root"), SubPath("rel"), Param("stem")
module = root / "src" / rel / T(t"{stem}.py")

>>> module
PathExpr('{root}/src/{rel...}/{stem}.py')
>>> module.render(root="/home/a/project", rel="pkg/sub", stem="io")
'/home/a/project/src/pkg/sub/io.py'
>>> module.render(root="project", rel="", stem="setup")
'project/src/setup.py'
>>> module.render(root="project", rel="../..", stem="setup")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.InvalidBindingError: rel='../..' must not contain '..'

The pattern writes a sub-path as {rel...}. An empty sub-path contributes no segments. An absolute parameter rejects a relative value:

>>> home = Absolute("home")
>>> (home / ".config").render(home="/home/a")
'/home/a/.config'
>>> (home / ".config").render(home="home/a")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.InvalidBindingError: home='home/a' must be an absolute path

Kinds apply to path operands. A parameter inside a formatted field, such as {stem} in t"{stem}.py", contributes formatted text to one segment, and that text cannot contain a / (Expressions).

items.title: Type, choices and default
items.text:
split = Segment("split", choices={"train", "test"})
idx = Param("idx", type=int)
total = Param("total", type=int, default=100)

shard = P("data") / split / T(t"chunk_{idx:04d}-of-{total:04d}.parquet")
  • type= is checked with isinstance when a value is bound. It also tells match how to read text back, so idx matches as an int. Param and Segment take type=. SubPath, AnyPath and Absolute bind paths, so they do not.
  • choices= lists the accepted values. match reads only those values, which can make a path that would otherwise be ambiguous readable in one way (Rendering and matching).
  • default= is the value used when a path is rendered without a binding for the name.
>>> shard.render(split="train", idx=7)
'data/train/chunk_0007-of-0100.parquet'
>>> shard.render(split="val", idx=7)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.InvalidBindingError: split='val': not one of {'test', 'train'}
>>> shard.match("data/test/chunk_0003-of-0100.parquet")
Match('data/test/chunk_0003-of-0100.parquet', {'split': 'test', 'idx': 3, 'total': 100})
>>> sorted(shard.required_params())
['idx', 'split']

A default is part of the declaration, and is checked against the type, choices and kind when the parameter is declared. It is used when a path is rendered, and nowhere else:

  • bind leaves a defaulted parameter free. defaults gives the defaults by name, and shard.bind(shard.defaults) applies them.
  • match reads every part from the path, so a default never makes a part optional.
  • glob finds a defaulted parameter's values on disk, and does not fix it to its default.
>>> shard.bind(shard.defaults)
PathExpr('data/{split}/chunk_{idx:04d}-of-0100.parquet')
>>> print(shard.match("data/test/chunk_0003.parquet"))
None

Two different declarations under one name in one expression raise ParamConflictError.

items.title: Why a segment cannot traverse
items.text:
A segment parameter's value must be exactly one segment: it contains no /, and it is not "", . or ... Each of those would change the path's structure, so a value bound to a segment parameter always names one entry of the directory before it. A sub-path parameter has the same property: its value is relative and contains no ...

So untrusted input, such as a file name from a request, can be bound to a Param after the head, a Segment or a SubPath: no value bound to it takes the rendered path outside a literal base before it. SEMANTICS.md §8 records that this is tested with random expressions and operations.

A Param at the head and an AnyPath accept any path, and an Absolute accepts any absolute path. A value bound to one of them can lead anywhere. To keep such a path below a base, declare Under on it (Effects).

items.title: A joined str is a trusted literal
items.text:
A str joined with / is part of the expression's literal text, with pathlib's rules. Its .. segments are kept, and an absolute str replaces everything before it:

>>> asset / "../../etc"
PathExpr('/srv/static/{name}/../../etc')
>>> asset / "/etc"
PathExpr('/etc')

Literal text is part of the program. Bind untrusted values to a parameter, and do not join them.

items.title: Relations
items.text:
from wend import P, Param, T

root, name = Param("root"), Param("name")
data = P(root) / "data" / T(t"{name}.csv")
schema = data.sibling("schema.json")
report = data.cousin("../reports", T(t"{name}.md"))

>>> schema
PathExpr('{root}/data/schema.json')
>>> report
PathExpr('{root}/reports/{name}.md')
>>> moved = data.rebase(P(root) / "data", P("/archive") / "2026")
>>> moved
PathExpr('/archive/2026/{name}.csv')
>>> schema.rebase(data, moved)
PathExpr('/archive/2026/schema.json')
>>> report.rebase(data, moved)
PathExpr('/archive/reports/{name}.md')

schema and report are defined by data. Moving data to /archive/2026 and rebasing them onto the moved path recomputes them from it: the sibling stays next to the data file, and the cousin stays one directory up.

items.title: Derivations
items.text:
Each expression records the public operation that built it and the arguments it was given: its derivation. The derivation is not part of the path. Equality, hashing, rendering and matching ignore it:

>>> schema == P(root) / "data" / "schema.json"
True
>>> schema.derived_from(data)
True
>>> (P(root) / "data" / "schema.json").derived_from(data)
False

derived_from reports whether an expression was built from another one.

items.title: Base and relative part
items.text:
A join records its left operand as its base and its right operand as its base_rel. x / y, x.child(y) and y.under(x) are all joins. Bases chain, one per join:

>>> config = P(root).child("config.yaml")
>>> config.base, config.base_rel
(PathExpr('{root}'), PathExpr('config.yaml'))
>>> data.base
PathExpr('{root}/data')
>>> data.base.base
PathExpr('{root}')

items.title: Siblings and cousins
items.text:
• sibling(n) is parent / n.
  • cousin(p, *names) starts at parent. Each component of the relative path p is either .., which takes the parent, or a name, which is joined. Then each of names is joined.

Both are computed from the structure, so they need no bindings. A cousin with an absolute p raises PathOperationError.

items.title: Rebasing
items.text:
rebase takes one or two arguments:

  • rebase(new) replaces the base of a join: config.rebase(P("/etc/app")) is /etc/app/config.yaml.
  • rebase(old, new) rebuilds the expression with new in place of every expression in its derivation that equals old, and applies each recorded operation again. The result equals building the expression from scratch with new in place of old.
>>> config.rebase(P("/etc/app"))
PathExpr('/etc/app/config.yaml')
>>> report.rebase(root, P("/srv"))
PathExpr('/srv/reports/{name}.md')

If old is not in the derivation, it must be a structural prefix of the expression, and the result is new joined with the rest of the path. relative_to gives that rest:

>>> data.relative_to(root)
PathExpr('data/{name}.csv')

items.title: One fragment, many bases
items.text:
under places a relative expression below a base. One fragment can be placed under several bases, and each result keeps the base it was given:

>>> cache = P("cache") / "models"
>>> [cache.under(home) for home in ("/home/a/.app", "/home/b/.app")]
[PathExpr('/home/a/.app/cache/models'), PathExpr('/home/b/.app/cache/models')]
>>> cache.under(root)
PathExpr('{root}/cache/models')
>>> cache.under(root).base
PathExpr('{root}')

items.title: Installation
items.text:
wend needs Python 3.14 or later. Its expressions are built from template strings (t-strings), which PEP 750 added in Python 3.14.

pip install wend

With uv, add it to a project:

uv add wend

The core package has no dependencies.

items.title: Extras
items.text:
Each optional integration is an extra, which installs the library it needs.

extra installs enables pydantic Pydantic wend.pydantic.PathOf: path fields on Pydantic models, validated against an expression fsspec fsspec wend.fs.FsspecFS and wend.fs.url_to_fs: glob and infer on object stores and other fsspec filesystems polars Polars wend.frame.resolve_frame: render one expression for every row of a DataFrame 
pip install "wend[polars]"
uv add "wend[pydantic,fsspec]"

The fsspec extra installs fsspec alone. A store's own backend, such as s3fs for S3 or gcsfs for Google Cloud Storage, is installed separately.

items.title: Checking the installation
items.text:
>>> from wend import Param, T
>>> name = Param("name")
>>> T(t"data/{name}.csv").render(name="trips")
'data/trips.csv'

On an earlier Python, t"..." is a syntax error.

items.title: Quickstart
items.text: This page builds one expression for a dataset stored as numbered chunks, and uses it in each direction. It needs Python 3.14 and wend, with no extras (Installation). The examples build on each other: run them in order, in an empty directory.

items.title: Build an expression
items.text:
from wend import Param, Segment, T

root = Param("root")
split = Segment("split", choices={"train", "test"})
idx = Param("idx", type=int)

shard = root / split / T(t"chunk_{idx:04d}.parquet")
  • Param declares a parameter: a named part of the path that gets its value later. type=int says that idx holds integers.
  • Segment declares a parameter that is exactly one path segment. choices= lists the values it accepts.
  • T makes an expression from a t-string. {idx:04d} is a formatted field: its format spec is kept and applied when the path is rendered.
  • / joins, as it does for pathlib.Path.

The result is a PathExpr. Its repr shows the structure it records:

>>> shard
PathExpr('{root}/{split}/chunk_{idx:04d}.parquet')

items.title: Render it
items.text:
render substitutes values and returns a string. resolve returns a pathlib.Path.

>>> shard.render(root="data", split="train", idx=7)
'data/train/chunk_0007.parquet'
>>> shard.resolve(root="data", split="train", idx=7)
PosixPath('data/train/chunk_0007.parquet')

Each value is checked against its declaration first:

>>> shard.render(root="data", split="train", idx="7")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.InvalidBindingError: idx='7': expected int

items.title: Match a path back
items.text:
match reads the values back out of a path. It returns a Match, a read-only mapping of names to typed values, or None when the expression does not describe the path.

>>> m = shard.match("data/test/chunk_0042.parquet")
>>> m
Match('data/test/chunk_0042.parquet', {'root': 'data', 'split': 'test', 'idx': 42})
>>> m["idx"]
42
>>> print(shard.match("data/val/chunk_0042.parquet"))
None

val is not one of the declared splits, so the second path has no match.

items.title: Find the files that exist
items.text:
First create a small tree: four chunks, a notes.txt and a val/ directory.

from pathlib import Path

for name in [
    "train/chunk_0000.parquet",
    "train/chunk_0001.parquet",
    "train/chunk_0003.parquet",
    "train/notes.txt",
    "test/chunk_0000.parquet",
    "val/chunk_0000.parquet",
]:
    path = Path("data", name)
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    path.touch()

glob walks the tree along the expression's structure and yields a Match for each path the expression describes:

>>> for m in shard.glob(root="data"):
...     print(m["split"], m["idx"], m.path)
test 0 data/test/chunk_0000.parquet
train 0 data/train/chunk_0000.parquet
train 1 data/train/chunk_0001.parquet
train 3 data/train/chunk_0003.parquet

notes.txt and val/chunk_0000.parquet do not fit the expression, so they are not yielded. Bindings given to glob fix parameters before the walk, so the next call lists only data/train. Comparing what exists with what should exist finds a gap:

>>> found = {m["idx"] for m in shard.glob(root="data", split="train")}
>>> sorted(set(range(4)) - found)
[2]

items.title: Operate on it without values
items.text:
Path operations work on the expression itself, with no values bound.

>>> shard.parent
PathExpr('{root}/{split}')
>>> meta = shard.with_suffix(".json")
>>> meta
PathExpr('{root}/{split}/chunk_{idx:04d}.json')

A Match is a mapping, so the values read from one path render another:

>>> meta.render(shard.match("data/train/chunk_0003.parquet"))
'data/train/chunk_0003.json'

items.title: Check a condition
items.text:
render never looks at the filesystem. An expression can declare what must be true of its path when the path is used, and check tests that against the filesystem.

from wend import Exists, File

stored = shard.requires(File, Exists)

>>> stored.check(root="data", split="train", idx=1)
PosixPath('data/train/chunk_0001.parquet')
>>> stored.check(root="data", split="train", idx=2)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.MissingPathError: 'data/train/chunk_0002.parquet' does not exist (required: Exists)

MissingPathError is also a FileNotFoundError, so existing except FileNotFoundError handlers catch it.

items.title: Datasets and shards
items.text: A dataset is stored as numbered shards, in one directory per split. This guide declares that layout once, renders the paths a writer produces, lists the shards that exist and finds the ones that are missing. It needs Python 3.14 and wend, with no extras. The examples build on each other: run them in order, in an empty directory.

items.title: Declare the layout
items.text:
from wend import Param, Segment, counter

root = Param("root")
dataset = Segment("dataset")
split = Segment("split", choices={"train", "test"})
name = counter("shard", width=5, of_total=True, sep="-", suffix=".parquet")

shard = root / dataset / split / name

>>> name
PathExpr('shard-{idx:05d}-of-{total:05d}.parquet')
>>> shard
PathExpr('{root}/{dataset}/{split}/shard-{idx:05d}-of-{total:05d}.parquet')
>>> shard.render(root="data", dataset="tiny", split="train", idx=0, total=4)
'data/tiny/train/shard-00000-of-00004.parquet'
  • counter writes a counter filename. With of_total=True the name also holds the number of shards. Its parameters, idx and total, are integers formatted with 05d, so matching reads them back as int.
  • dataset and split are segments: each value is one directory name. split accepts only train and test.

counter returns an ordinary expression, equal to the same name written as a t-string:

>>> from wend import T
>>> idx, total = Param("idx", type=int), Param("total", type=int)
>>> name == T(t"shard-{idx:05d}-of-{total:05d}.parquet")
True

items.title: Render every expected path
items.text:
A writer knows the root, the dataset and the number of shards before it starts. bind fixes them once:

>>> layout = shard.bind(root="data", dataset="tiny", total=4)
>>> layout
PathExpr('data/tiny/{split}/shard-{idx:05d}-of-00004.parquet')

compile generates a Python function specialised to the expression, and caches it on the expression. Its many method renders one path for each mapping of bindings:

>>> compiled = layout.compile()
>>> rows = [{"split": s, "idx": i} for s in ("train", "test") for i in range(4)]
>>> paths = compiled.many(rows)
>>> len(paths)
8
>>> for path in paths[:3]:
...     print(path)
data/tiny/train/shard-00000-of-00004.parquet
data/tiny/train/shard-00001-of-00004.parquet
data/tiny/train/shard-00002-of-00004.parquet

columns takes the same bindings column by column, and calling the compiled renderer returns one pathlib.Path, as resolve does:

>>> for path in compiled.columns(split=["test", "test"], idx=range(2)):
...     print(path)
data/tiny/test/shard-00000-of-00004.parquet
data/tiny/test/shard-00001-of-00004.parquet
>>> compiled(split="test", idx=3)
PosixPath('data/tiny/test/shard-00003-of-00004.parquet')

A compiled renderer returns what render returns for the same bindings, and raises the same error for a value that render rejects:

>>> compiled.many([{"split": "val", "idx": 0}])
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.InvalidBindingError: split='val': not one of {'test', 'train'}

items.title: Render several paths per shard
items.text:
Each shard has a JSON file of metadata next to it, with the same name and the suffix .json. compile_many compiles several expressions into one function. In each call, every parameter is looked up, checked and formatted once, however many of the expressions use it.

>>> from wend import compile_many
>>> outputs = compile_many({"data": layout, "meta": layout.with_suffix(".json")})
>>> shard_0 = outputs.render(split="train", idx=0)
>>> shard_0["data"]
'data/tiny/train/shard-00000-of-00004.parquet'
>>> shard_0["meta"]
'data/tiny/train/shard-00000-of-00004.json'
>>> for data, meta in outputs.many(rows[:2]):
...     print(meta)
data/tiny/train/shard-00000-of-00004.json
data/tiny/train/shard-00001-of-00004.json

Given a dict, render returns a dict with the same keys. many returns one tuple per row, with the paths in the order the expressions were given.

items.title: Write some shards
items.text:
The next examples need shards on disk. This writes five of the eight shards, then two files that do not belong to layout: one named without the counter, and one left by an earlier write of three shards.

from pathlib import Path

written = [("train", 0), ("train", 1), ("train", 3), ("test", 0), ("test", 1)]
for path in compiled.many({"split": s, "idx": i} for s, i in written):
    Path(path).parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    Path(path).touch()

Path("data/tiny/train/shard-2.parquet").touch()
Path("data/tiny/test/shard-00002-of-00003.parquet").touch()

items.title: List the shards that exist
items.text:
glob walks the directories along the expression's structure and yields a Match for each existing path that the expression describes, in path order:

>>> for m in layout.glob():
...     print(m["split"], m["idx"], m.path)
test 0 data/tiny/test/shard-00000-of-00004.parquet
test 1 data/tiny/test/shard-00001-of-00004.parquet
train 0 data/tiny/train/shard-00000-of-00004.parquet
train 1 data/tiny/train/shard-00001-of-00004.parquet
train 3 data/tiny/train/shard-00003-of-00004.parquet

shard-2.parquet does not have the counter's form, and shard-00002-of-00003.parquet has a total of 3 where layout requires 4, so neither is yielded. Each idx is an int, read from the filename and checked by rendering it again.

items.title: Find the gaps
items.text:
The set of shards that should exist, minus the set that glob found, is the set of missing shards. The same layout renders their paths:

>>> expected = {(r["split"], r["idx"]) for r in rows}
>>> found = {(m["split"], m["idx"]) for m in layout.glob()}
>>> missing = sorted(expected - found)
>>> missing
[('test', 2), ('test', 3), ('train', 2)]
>>> for path in compiled.many({"split": s, "idx": i} for s, i in missing):
...     print(path)
data/tiny/test/shard-00002-of-00004.parquet
data/tiny/test/shard-00003-of-00004.parquet
data/tiny/train/shard-00002-of-00004.parquet

items.title: Find shards from another write
items.text:
layout fixes total. shard leaves it free, so glob reads the total from each filename, and shards written with a different total can be found:

>>> for m in shard.glob(root="data", dataset="tiny"):
...     if m["total"] != 4:
...         print(m.path, m["total"])
data/tiny/test/shard-00002-of-00003.parquet 3

Bindings given to glob fix those parameters before the walk, so this call lists only data/tiny.

items.title: Numbered files without a total
items.text:
A log directory grows one file at a time, so its names have no total. Without of_total, counter writes the index alone:

log = root / "logs" / counter("log", width=3, suffix=".jsonl")

Path("data/logs").mkdir()
for i in range(3):
    Path(log.render(root="data", idx=i)).touch()

>>> log
PathExpr('{root}/logs/log_{idx:03d}.jsonl')
>>> last = max(m["idx"] for m in log.glob(root="data"))
>>> log.render(root="data", idx=last + 1)
'data/logs/log_003.jsonl'

Without width, the index is not padded. A match must render back to the same path, so a padded name does not match an unpadded counter:

>>> part = counter("part", suffix=".csv")
>>> part
PathExpr('part_{idx:d}.csv')
>>> part.match("part_12.csv")
Match('part_12.csv', {'idx': 12})
>>> print(part.match("part_012.csv"))
None

items.title: Mapping between trees
items.text: A site generator turns each Markdown file under src/ into an HTML file at the same place under site/. This guide declares that relation once as a Lens, maps paths in both directions, and finds the pages that need building again. It needs Python 3.14 and wend, with no extras. The examples build on each other: run them in order, in an empty directory.

items.title: Declare the lens
items.text:
from wend import Lens, P, Param, SubPath, T

rel, stem = SubPath("rel"), Param("stem")
source = P("src") / rel / T(t"{stem}.md")
output = P("site") / rel / T(t"{stem}.html")

build = Lens(source, output)

The two expressions share the parameters rel and stem. rel is a SubPath: zero or more directory names. Calling the lens matches a path against the source and renders the bindings through the output:

>>> build
Lens('src/{rel...}/{stem}.md' -> 'site/{rel...}/{stem}.html')
>>> build("src/guide/install.md")
PosixPath('site/guide/install.html')
>>> build("src/index.md")
PosixPath('site/index.html')
>>> build.backward("site/guide/install.html")
PosixPath('src/guide/install.md')

backward maps the other way, from an output to its source. render returns the output as a str. A path that the source does not describe raises NoMatchError, a ValueError:

>>> from wend import NoMatchError
>>> try:
...     build("src/notes/todo.txt")
... except NoMatchError as e:
...     print(e)
'src/notes/todo.txt' does not match 'src/{rel...}/{stem}.md'

items.title: Map many paths
items.text:
Create a source tree with three pages and a file that is not a page:

from pathlib import Path

for name in ["index.md", "guide/install.md", "guide/usage.md", "notes/todo.txt"]:
    path = Path("src", name)
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    path.write_text(f"# {path.stem}\n")

map yields a pair (path, output) for each path that the source describes, in the order given, and skips the others:

>>> files = sorted(str(p) for p in Path("src").rglob("*") if p.is_file())
>>> for src, out in build.map(files):
...     print(src, "->", out)
src/guide/install.md -> site/guide/install.html
src/guide/usage.md -> site/guide/usage.html
src/index.md -> site/index.html

source.glob() finds the same pages directly, with their bindings:

>>> [m.path for m in source.glob()]
['src/guide/install.md', 'src/guide/usage.md', 'src/index.md']

items.title: Find stale outputs
items.text:
An output is stale when it does not exist, or when its source was modified after it. Build two of the pages, then edit one of their sources. The example sets the modification times with os.utime, so its result does not depend on how fast it runs.

import os

for src, out in build.map(["src/guide/install.md", "src/guide/usage.md"]):
    out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    out.write_text(f"<h1>{out.stem}</h1>\n")
    os.utime(src, (1_700_000_000, 1_700_000_000))
    os.utime(out, (1_700_000_060, 1_700_000_060))

os.utime("src/guide/usage.md", (1_700_000_120, 1_700_000_120))


def stale(src, out):
    return not out.exists() or out.stat().st_mtime < os.stat(src).st_mtime

>>> [src for src, out in build.map(m.path for m in source.glob()) if stale(src, out)]
['src/guide/usage.md', 'src/index.md']

index.md has never been built, and usage.md changed after its page was built.

items.title: Find outputs with no source
items.text:
An output whose source was deleted is left behind. inverse is the lens in the other direction, so mapping every output through it gives each one's source:

Path("site/old.html").write_text("<h1>old</h1>\n")

>>> pages = [m.path for m in output.glob()]
>>> pages
['site/guide/install.html', 'site/guide/usage.html', 'site/old.html']
>>> [out for out, src in build.inverse().map(pages) if not src.exists()]
['site/old.html']

items.title: Parameters only the output has
items.text:
An output can have parameters that the source does not. They are bound in each call, by keyword or in a mapping after the path:

>>> versioned = Lens(source, P("site") / Param("version") / rel / T(t"{stem}.html"))
>>> versioned("src/index.md", version="1.2")
PosixPath('site/1.2/index.html')
>>> versioned.backward("site/1.2/guide/install.html")
PosixPath('src/guide/install.md')
>>> versioned("src/index.md")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.MissingBindingError: Missing bindings: ['version']

items.title: Two sources for one target
items.text:
A lens whose two sides have the same parameters is lossless (lossless): each side gives all the bindings the other needs. A lossless lens checks that each output it renders reads back in exactly one way, so that it maps back to a single source. This lens flattens each section into the file name:

>>> section = Param("section")
>>> page = P("src") / section / T(t"{stem}.md")
>>> flat = P("flat") / T(t"{section}-{stem}.html")
>>> flatten = Lens(page, flat)
>>> flatten.lossless
True
>>> flatten("src/api/read.md")
PosixPath('flat/api-read.html')
>>> flatten("src/api/io-read.md")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.AmbiguousMatchError: 'flat/api-io-read.html' matches ambiguously: {'section': 'api', 'stem': 'io-read'}, {'section': 'api-io', 'stem': 'read'}. ...

src/api/io-read.md and src/api-io/read.md would both map to flat/api-io-read.html, so the lens raises AmbiguousMatchError for either of them. It raises whether or not the other source exists, because the output path alone cannot say which source it came from.

Declaring the sections with choices= leaves one reading:

>>> from wend import Segment
>>> section = Segment("section", choices={"api", "guide"})
>>> page = P("src") / section / T(t"{stem}.md")
>>> flat = P("flat") / T(t"{section}-{stem}.html")
>>> flatten = Lens(page, flat)
>>> flatten("src/api/io-read.md")
PosixPath('flat/api-io-read.html')
>>> flatten.backward("flat/api-io-read.html")
PosixPath('src/api/io-read.md')

map takes ambiguous= with the same values as glob: "raise" (the default), "skip", or a callable that receives each error, such as report.append.

  • API reference: Lens, Lens.map, NoMatchError, AmbiguousMatchError.

items.title: Lineage and caching
items.text: A path has two histories. The expression records how the path was built from other paths, and the files record which ones were made from which. This guide reads the first with explain and tags, records the second with a Ledger, uses it to find what is out of date, and names cache entries after the contents of their inputs. It needs Python 3.14 and wend, with no extras. The examples build on each other: run them in order, in an empty directory.

items.title: How an expression was built
items.text:
A pipeline cleans a day's raw upload and writes a report from the clean copy. Each path is defined from the one before it:

from wend import P, Param, T
from wend.lineage import explain, tags

root, day = Param("root"), Param("day")

raw = (P(root) / "raw" / T(t"{day}.csv")).tag(source="upload")
clean = raw.cousin("../clean", T(t"{day}.csv")).tag(stage="clean")
report = clean.cousin("../reports", T(t"{day}.md"))

Each expression records the operation that built it and its arguments: its derivation (Relations). explain writes the derivation out, one operation per line, sources first:

>>> print(explain(report))
{root}/raw = join({root}, 'raw')
{root}/raw/{day}.csv = join({root}/raw, {day}.csv)
{root}/clean/{day}.csv = cousin({root}/raw/{day}.csv, '../clean', {day}.csv)
{root}/reports/{day}.md = cousin({root}/clean/{day}.csv, '../reports', {day}.md)

tag attaches metadata to one expression, which keeps it in PathExpr.tags. tags collects the tags of an expression and of every expression it was built from. Where two set the same name, the nearer one wins.

>>> dict(clean.tags), dict(report.tags)
({'stage': 'clean'}, {})
>>> tags(report)
{'source': 'upload', 'stage': 'clean'}

Like conditions, the derivation and the tags are not part of the path. report equals the same path built directly, and bind keeps the tags:

>>> report == P(root) / "reports" / T(t"{day}.md")
True
>>> tags(report.bind(root="data"))
{'source': 'upload', 'stage': 'clean'}

items.title: Record what each step made
items.text:
Each step is a Step whose conditions say which paths it reads and which it creates (Pipeline steps):

from pathlib import Path

from wend import Absent, Creatable, Exists, File, Readable, Step
from wend.lineage import Ledger

clean_step = Step(
    raw=raw.requires(File, Exists, Readable),
    clean=clean.requires(Absent, Creatable).ensures(File, Exists),
)
report_step = Step(
    clean=clean.requires(File, Exists, Readable),
    report=report.requires(Absent, Creatable).ensures(File, Exists),
)

Path("data/raw").mkdir(parents=True)
Path("data/raw/mon.csv").write_text("id,value\n1,3\n2,4\n")
ledger = Ledger("data/lineage.jsonl")

A Ledger is an append-only file of JSON lines. run runs a step as with step(...) does. When the step succeeds, it records each path the step declares it creates, writes or deletes as made from the paths it declares it reads, with a digest of each file's contents:

with ledger.run(clean_step, root="data", day="mon") as p:
    p["clean"].parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    p["clean"].write_text(p["raw"].read_text().replace(",", "\t"))

with ledger.run(report_step, root="data", day="mon") as p:
    p["report"].parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    rows = p["clean"].read_text().splitlines()[1:]
    p["report"].write_text(f"{len(rows)} rows\n")

>>> len(ledger.records())
2

items.title: Ask where a file came from
items.text:
The ledger stores absolute paths. rel shortens them for display:

import os


def rel(paths):
    return [os.path.relpath(p) for p in paths]

provenance gives a file's latest Record: its inputs, the step, the bindings it used, and the tags of the expression it was rendered from.

>>> record = ledger.provenance("data/reports/mon.md")
>>> rel(path for path, digest in record.inputs)
['data/clean/mon.csv']
>>> record.operation
"Step(clean='{root}/clean/{day}.csv', report='{root}/reports/{day}.md')"
>>> record.bindings
{'root': 'data', 'day': 'mon'}
>>> record.tags
{'source': 'upload', 'stage': 'clean'}

upstream follows the records back to every file a file was made from, nearest first. downstream follows them forward to every file made from a file:

>>> rel(ledger.upstream("data/reports/mon.md"))
['data/clean/mon.csv', 'data/raw/mon.csv']
>>> rel(ledger.downstream("data/raw/mon.csv"))
['data/clean/mon.csv', 'data/reports/mon.md']

items.title: Find what is stale
items.text:
The upload is corrected:

Path("data/raw/mon.csv").write_text("id,value\n1,3\n2,5\n")

stale reads the inputs of a file's latest record now, and lists those whose contents no longer match the recorded digests, or that are gone:

>>> rel(ledger.stale("data/clean/mon.csv"))
['data/raw/mon.csv']
>>> ledger.stale("data/reports/mon.md")
[]

The report is not stale by itself: its one input, the clean file, has not changed yet. stale looks at direct inputs only. downstream gives everything that depends on the changed file, which is what to build again:

>>> rel(ledger.downstream("data/raw/mon.csv"))
['data/clean/mon.csv', 'data/reports/mon.md']

wend records the relations. The order to build in, and the building, are left to the caller or to a workflow tool.

items.title: Name a cache entry after its input
items.text:
A content-addressed path is named after what it was computed from. content_key reads files and returns a short digest of their contents. The key is bound to an ordinary parameter, so render stays pure:

import json

from wend.lineage import content_key

key = Param("key")
summary = P(root) / "cache" / key / "summary.json"


def cached_summary(src):
    out = summary.resolve(root="data", key=content_key(src))
    if not out.exists():
        print("computing", out)
        rows = Path(src).read_text().splitlines()[1:]
        out.parent.mkdir(parents=True)
        out.write_text(json.dumps({"rows": len(rows)}))
    return out

The first call computes the summary. The second call, with the same input, finds it:

>>> first = cached_summary("data/raw/mon.csv")
computing data/cache/28c614b91d6d0aec/summary.json
>>> cached_summary("data/raw/mon.csv") == first
True

match reads the key back out of a cached path. Whether the entry still names its input is a check made now, by computing the key again:

>>> summary.match(first)["key"] == content_key("data/raw/mon.csv")
True

After another change to the upload, the key differs, and the next call computes a new entry:

Path("data/raw/mon.csv").write_text("id,value\n1,3\n2,5\n3,8\n")

>>> summary.match(first)["key"] == content_key("data/raw/mon.csv")
False
>>> cached_summary("data/raw/mon.csv")
computing data/cache/df0124d58739da13/summary.json
PosixPath('data/cache/df0124d58739da13/summary.json')

values_key gives a key for values, such as the settings a result depends on. It reads no files, and the order of the keywords does not change it:

>>> from wend.lineage import values_key
>>> values_key(model="tiny", epochs=3)
'74341c5f7f50e110'
>>> values_key(epochs=3, model="tiny")
'74341c5f7f50e110'

items.title: Pipeline steps
items.text: A pipeline step reads a day's raw readings, drops the rows with no value, and writes a clean copy. This guide declares what the step needs before it runs and what it promises afterwards, runs it as a Step, and shows what happens when it runs again or fails. It needs Python 3.14 and wend, with no extras. The examples build on each other: run them in order, in an empty directory.

items.title: Declare the paths and their conditions
items.text:
from wend import Absent, Creatable, Exists, File, P, Param, Readable, Step, T

root, day = Param("root"), Param("day")

raw = (P(root) / "raw" / T(t"{day}.csv")).requires(File, Exists, Readable)
clean = (P(root) / "clean" / T(t"{day}.csv")).requires(Absent, Creatable)
clean = clean.ensures(File, Exists)

convert = Step(raw=raw, clean=clean)
  • requires declares preconditions. The raw file must be an existing, readable file. Nothing may be at the clean path yet, and it must be possible to create it.
  • ensures declares postconditions: after the step, the clean path is an existing file.
  • Step groups the paths that one step uses, by name. Its bindings are shared, and each path takes the parameters it uses.

effects lists what each path is declared to be used for:

>>> convert
Step(raw='{root}/raw/{day}.csv', clean='{root}/clean/{day}.csv')
>>> convert.effects()
[<raw: read {root}/raw/{day}.csv>, <clean: create {root}/clean/{day}.csv>]

read comes from Readable, and create from Creatable. A path that must exist afterwards and need not exist before is also listed as create. The list reports the declarations. It does not observe what the step's code does.

items.title: Write the transform
items.text:
The transform is ordinary code that takes two pathlib.Path values:

import csv
from pathlib import Path


def drop_missing(src: Path, dst: Path) -> None:
    with src.open(newline="") as f:
        rows = [row for row in csv.DictReader(f) if row["temp_c"].strip()]
    dst.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    with dst.open("w", newline="") as f:
        out = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=["station", "temp_c"])
        out.writeheader()
        out.writerows(rows)


Path("data/raw").mkdir(parents=True)
Path("data/raw/2026-10-17.csv").write_text("station,temp_c\nA,11.5\nB,\nC,9.0\n")

items.title: Run the step
items.text:
Calling the step with bindings gives a context manager. Entering it checks every precondition and gives the rendered paths, as a dict keyed by the names given to Step. Leaving it without an exception checks every postcondition.

>>> with convert(root="data", day="2026-10-17") as p:
...     print(p)
...     drop_missing(p["raw"], p["clean"])
{'raw': PosixPath('data/raw/2026-10-17.csv'), 'clean': PosixPath('data/clean/2026-10-17.csv')}
>>> print(Path("data/clean/2026-10-17.csv").read_text())
station,temp_c
A,11.5
C,9.0
<BLANKLINE>

items.title: Run it a second time
items.text:
The clean file now exists, and the step requires it to be absent. The second run raises before the body runs, so the output is not overwritten:

>>> with convert(root="data", day="2026-10-17") as p:
...     drop_missing(p["raw"], p["clean"])
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.PathExistsError: 'data/clean/2026-10-17.csv' already exists (required: Absent)

PathExistsError is also a FileExistsError. A loop over every day with input can run the step for each one and skip the days already done. glob yields a Match for each raw file, and a Match is a mapping of bindings, so it can be passed to the step:

Path("data/raw/2026-10-18.csv").write_text("station,temp_c\nA,12.0\nB,10.5\n")

>>> for m in raw.glob(root="data"):
...     try:
...         with convert(m) as p:
...             drop_missing(p["raw"], p["clean"])
...     except FileExistsError:
...         print("skipped", m["day"])
...     else:
...         print("converted", m["day"])
skipped 2026-10-17
converted 2026-10-18

items.title: A missing input
items.text:
A day with no raw file fails on entry, with MissingPathError, a FileNotFoundError:

>>> with convert(root="data", day="2026-10-19") as p:
...     drop_missing(p["raw"], p["clean"])
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.MissingPathError: 'data/raw/2026-10-19.csv' does not exist (required: Exists)

check runs the same checks without a body, and returns the rendered paths. Once the input exists, they pass:

Path("data/raw/2026-10-19.csv").write_text("station,temp_c\n")

>>> convert.check(root="data", day="2026-10-19")
{'raw': PosixPath('data/raw/2026-10-19.csv'), 'clean': PosixPath('data/clean/2026-10-19.csv')}

items.title: A body that does not write its output
items.text:
If the body finishes without creating the clean file, the postcondition fails when the block is left:

>>> with convert(root="data", day="2026-10-19") as p:
...     pass
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.MissingPathError: 'data/clean/2026-10-19.csv' does not exist (required: Exists)

If the body raises, its exception propagates and the postconditions are not checked. confirm checks the postconditions on their own.

items.title: A step that replaces its output
items.text:
To let a step overwrite its output, declare Writable in place of Absent and Creatable. Writable holds for an existing path that can be written, or for one that can be created.

>>> from wend import Writable
>>> output = (P(root) / "clean" / T(t"{day}.csv")).requires(Writable)
>>> rebuild = Step(raw=raw, clean=output.ensures(File, Exists))
>>> rebuild.effects()
[<raw: read {root}/raw/{day}.csv>, <clean: create, write {root}/clean/{day}.csv>]
>>> with rebuild(root="data", day="2026-10-17") as p:
...     drop_missing(p["raw"], p["clean"])

items.title: What the checks guarantee
items.text: Each check describes the filesystem at the moment it runs. A file that exists when the step is entered can be removed before the body opens it, and the checks are not atomic with the body's reads and writes. The conditions state what the step expects and catch mistakes such as a missing input or an output that would be overwritten (Effects).
