items.title: Settings and anchors
items.text: An application declares where its files live once, at module level, and binds the values when it starts, from its settings. This guide gives parameters defaults, binds them from settings objects, overrides them with keywords, and starts paths from the standard directories: the home directory, the working directory and the XDG base directories. It needs Python 3.14 and wend, with no extras. The Pydantic example also needs Pydantic, which the pydantic extra installs (Installation). The examples build on each other: run them in order.

items.title: Declare the paths, with defaults
items.text:
from wend import Param, Segment, T

root = Param("root")
env = Segment("env", choices={"dev", "prod"}, default="dev")
version = Param("version", type=int, default=1)

CONFIG = root / "config" / T(t"{env}.toml")
MODEL = root / "models" / T(t"v{version}") / Param("model")

A parameter with default= takes that value when a path is rendered without a binding for it:

>>> CONFIG.render(root="/srv/app")
'/srv/app/config/dev.toml'
>>> CONFIG.render(root="/srv/app", env="prod")
'/srv/app/config/prod.toml'
>>> MODEL.defaults
{'version': 1}
>>> sorted(MODEL.required_params())
['model', 'root']

defaults gives the defaults by name, and required_params the parameters that must be bound. Defaults apply when a path is rendered and nowhere else: bind leaves a defaulted parameter free, and match and glob read its value from the path (Parameters).

items.title: Bind from a dataclass
items.text:
Every method that takes a mapping of bindings also takes an object whose fields are named after the parameters:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path


@dataclass
class Settings:
    root: Path
    env: str = "prod"
    workers: int = 4

>>> settings = Settings(Path("/srv/app"))
>>> CONFIG.resolve(settings)
PosixPath('/srv/app/config/prod.toml')

The field env is a binding, so its value prod is used in place of the parameter's default. wend.bindings shows what an object binds. Fields that no expression uses, such as workers, are ignored where the bindings are used.

>>> from wend import bindings
>>> bindings(settings)
{'root': PosixPath('/srv/app'), 'env': 'prod', 'workers': 4}

items.title: Override with keywords
items.text:
Keyword bindings take precedence over an object's fields:

>>> CONFIG.render(settings, env="dev")
'/srv/app/config/dev.toml'
>>> bindings(settings, env="dev")
{'root': PosixPath('/srv/app'), 'env': 'dev', 'workers': 4}

items.title: Bind from a named tuple
items.text:
A named tuple binds its fields in the same way:

from typing import NamedTuple


class Job(NamedTuple):
    root: str
    model: str
    version: int = 2

>>> MODEL.render(Job("/srv/app", "bert"))
'/srv/app/models/v2/bert'

items.title: Bind from a Pydantic model
items.text:
A Pydantic model binds its fields. Properties, methods and computed fields bind nothing, so a computed field can render a path from its own model:

from pydantic import BaseModel, computed_field


class AppSettings(BaseModel):
    root: Path
    env: str = "dev"

    @computed_field
    @property
    def config(self) -> Path:
        return CONFIG.resolve(self)

>>> app = AppSettings(root="/srv/app")
>>> app.config
PosixPath('/srv/app/config/dev.toml')
>>> bindings(app)
{'root': PosixPath('/srv/app'), 'env': 'dev'}

attrs classes, and any other object with instance attributes, bind the same way (SEMANTICS.md §3.2). A class, or a path given in place of the bindings, raises TypeError:

>>> CONFIG.render("/srv/app")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
TypeError: Cannot take bindings from '/srv/app': bind a path by name, e.g. render(root=path), or pass a mapping

items.title: Start from a standard directory
items.text:
wend.anchors provides the directories a path usually starts from: HOME, CWD and the XDG base directories in XDG. Each is an Absolute parameter named after its environment variable, so an expression built on one stays symbolic:

>>> from wend import P
>>> from wend.anchors import CWD, HOME, XDG
>>> models = (P("models") / Param("model")).under(XDG.CACHE_HOME / "myapp")
>>> models
PathExpr('{XDG_CACHE_HOME}/myapp/models/{model}')
>>> HOME / ".myapp.toml"
PathExpr('{HOME}/.myapp.toml')

An anchor is bound like any parameter, which is how a test points the application at a temporary directory. An absolute path is required:

>>> models.render(XDG_CACHE_HOME="/tmp/test-cache", model="bert")
'/tmp/test-cache/myapp/models/bert'
>>> models.render(XDG_CACHE_HOME="cache", model="bert")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.InvalidBindingError: XDG_CACHE_HOME='cache' must be an absolute path

items.title: Read the anchors from the environment
items.text:
anchors.bindings reads every anchor's value at the moment it is called. render never reads the environment itself. With no argument it reads os.environ. Given a mapping, it reads that instead:

>>> from wend import anchors
>>> here = anchors.bindings({"HOME": "/home/ada"})
>>> for name, value in here.items():
...     if name != "CWD":
...         print(name, value)
HOME /home/ada
XDG_CONFIG_HOME /home/ada/.config
XDG_DATA_HOME /home/ada/.local/share
XDG_STATE_HOME /home/ada/.local/state
XDG_CACHE_HOME /home/ada/.cache
>>> models.render(here, model="bert")
'/home/ada/.cache/myapp/models/bert'
  • An XDG variable that is set to an absolute path is used. One that is unset, empty or relative falls back to its default below the home directory, as the XDG specification requires.
  • HOME is $HOME, or the home directory from the password database.
  • CWD is os.getcwd() when bindings is called.
>>> models.render(
...     anchors.bindings({"HOME": "/home/ada", "XDG_CACHE_HOME": "/var/cache/ada"}),
...     model="bert",
... )
'/var/cache/ada/myapp/models/bert'
>>> models.render(
...     anchors.bindings({"HOME": "/home/ada", "XDG_CACHE_HOME": "cache"}), model="bert"
... )
'/home/ada/.cache/myapp/models/bert'
>>> import os
>>> anchors.bindings()["CWD"] == os.getcwd()
True

The expression stays symbolic, so a path below an anchor matches back to the anchor's value:

>>> models.match("/home/ada/.cache/myapp/models/bert")
Match('/home/ada/.cache/myapp/models/bert', {'XDG_CACHE_HOME': '/home/ada/.cache', 'model': 'bert'})

The XDG anchors follow the XDG specification on every POSIX platform, macOS included. For a platform's own conventions, such as ~/Library/Caches on macOS, bind the anchor to the directory that a library such as platformdirs reports.

  • SEMANTICS.md §3.1 (defaults) and §3.2 (environments).
  • API reference: wend.bindings, PathExpr.defaults, wend.anchors.

items.title: Untrusted input
items.text: A web service stores the files that users upload, an import job unpacks the archives they send, and a configuration file names extra files to read. Each of these puts text from outside the program into a path. This guide declares where each value may go, so that a value that would lead elsewhere is rejected. It needs Python 3.14 and wend, with no extras. The examples build on each other: run them in order, in an empty directory.

items.title: Bind, never join
items.text:
pathlib joins a value as it is written, .. included:

>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> name = "../../../etc/passwd"
>>> Path("srv/uploads") / "ada" / name
PosixPath('srv/uploads/ada/../../../etc/passwd')

In wend, a value goes into a path by being bound to a parameter:

from wend import P, Param

root, user, filename = Param("root"), Param("user"), Param("filename")
upload = P(root) / "uploads" / user / filename

>>> upload.render(root="srv", user="ada", filename="cv.pdf")
'srv/uploads/ada/cv.pdf'
>>> upload.render(root="srv", user="ada", filename=name)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.InvalidBindingError: filename='../../../etc/passwd' is not a single path segment; declare 'filename' with SubPath('filename') to bind multi-segment paths

A str joined with / is different: it becomes part of the expression's literal text, with pathlib's rules, as the program's own text does:

>>> P("srv/uploads") / "ada" / name
PathExpr('srv/uploads/ada/../../../etc/passwd')

Literal text is trusted. Bind every value from outside the program to a parameter, and never join it.

items.title: One directory entry: segments
items.text:
user and filename come after the head of the expression, so each is a segment parameter: its value must be exactly one path segment. A value that contains a /, or is "", . or .., would change the structure of the path, and is rejected:

>>> from wend import InvalidBindingError
>>> for name in ["cv.pdf", "a/b.pdf", "/etc/passwd", "..", "", "x\x00y"]:
...     try:
...         print("ok:", upload.render(root="srv", user="ada", filename=name))
...     except InvalidBindingError as e:
...         print("rejected:", e)
ok: srv/uploads/ada/cv.pdf
rejected: filename='a/b.pdf' is not a single path segment; declare 'filename' with SubPath('filename') to bind multi-segment paths
rejected: filename='/etc/passwd' is not a single path segment; declare 'filename' with SubPath('filename') to bind multi-segment paths
rejected: filename='..' is not a valid path segment
rejected: filename='' is not a valid path segment
rejected: filename='x\x00y': contains NUL

So a value bound to a segment parameter always names one entry of the directory before it. InvalidBindingError is a ValueError.

A parameter inside a formatted field, such as {stem} in t"{stem}.png", contributes text to one segment, and that text cannot contain a / either:

>>> from wend import T
>>> stem = Param("stem")
>>> avatar = P(root) / "avatars" / user / T(t"{stem}.png")
>>> avatar.render(root="srv", user="ada", stem="../../x")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.InvalidBindingError: {stem} formats '../../x' to '../../x', which contains a separator

items.title: Nested names: SubPath
items.text:
The names in an archive have directories, so they need more than one segment. A SubPath parameter accepts a relative path of zero or more segments, without ... Create an archive with two ordinary members and two that point outside the target directory:

import zipfile

with zipfile.ZipFile("upload.zip", "w") as zf:
    zf.writestr("docs/readme.txt", "hello\n")
    zf.writestr("docs/img/logo.svg", "<svg/>\n")
    zf.writestr("../../.bashrc", "echo hi\n")
    zf.writestr("/etc/cron.d/job", "* * * * * root true\n")

Extract it through an expression, skipping each member whose name is rejected:

from wend import SubPath

member = P("extracted") / SubPath("member")


def extract(archive):
    with zipfile.ZipFile(archive) as zf:
        for info in zf.infolist():
            try:
                path = member.resolve(member=info.filename)
            except InvalidBindingError as e:
                print("skipped:", e)
                continue
            path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
            path.write_bytes(zf.read(info))
            print("wrote:", path)

>>> extract("upload.zip")
wrote: extracted/docs/readme.txt
wrote: extracted/docs/img/logo.svg
skipped: member='../../.bashrc' must not contain '..'
skipped: member='/etc/cron.d/job' must be a relative path

A sub-path containing .. is rejected even where the result would stay inside, as a/../b would.

items.title: A fixed set of values: choices
items.text:
Where the valid values are known in advance, list them with choices=:

>>> from wend import Segment
>>> area = Segment("area", choices={"avatars", "documents"})
>>> stored = P(root) / area / user / filename
>>> stored.render(root="srv", area="documents", user="ada", filename="cv.pdf")
'srv/documents/ada/cv.pdf'
>>> stored.render(root="srv", area="config", user="ada", filename="cv.pdf")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.InvalidBindingError: area='config': not one of {'avatars', 'documents'}

items.title: Path and absolute parameters: Under
items.text:
A parameter at the head of an expression, an AnyPath and an Absolute accept a whole path, which can lead anywhere. To keep such a path below a base, declare Under on the expression. render checks it against the rendered path, lexically, with no filesystem access:

>>> from wend import AnyPath, Under
>>> extra = (P(root) / AnyPath("rel")).requires(Under(P(root)))
>>> extra.render(root="/data", rel="lookups/zones.csv")
'/data/lookups/zones.csv'
>>> extra.render(root="/data", rel="/etc/passwd")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.ContainmentError: '/etc/passwd' is not under '/data' (required: Under('{root}'))
>>> extra.render(root="/data", rel="lookups/../../etc/passwd")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.ContainmentError: '/data/lookups/../../etc/passwd' is not under '/data' (required: Under('{root}'))

The rule is conservative: a path with a .. after the base is not under it, even when the .. would stay inside. An Absolute parameter also rejects a relative value:

>>> from wend import Absolute
>>> export = P(Absolute("export")).requires(Under(P("/data/exports")))
>>> export.render(export="/data/exports/2026-10")
'/data/exports/2026-10'
>>> export.render(export="/etc")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.ContainmentError: '/etc' is not under '/data/exports' (required: Under('/data/exports'))
>>> export.render(export="exports/2026-10")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.InvalidBindingError: export='exports/2026-10' must be an absolute path

ContainmentError is an InvalidBindingError, so one except ValueError handles every rejected value on this page.

items.title: What is and is not a sandbox
items.text: The rules above are about the text of a path. Every rendering checks them, and SEMANTICS.md §8 records how each is guaranteed or tested. The filesystem can still lead elsewhere through a symlink, and it can change after a check.

items.title: Symlinks
items.text:
Create an upload directory that holds a symlink to a directory outside it:

import os

Path("srv/uploads/ada").mkdir(parents=True)
Path("srv/uploads/ada/cv.pdf").write_text("%PDF\n")
Path("private").mkdir()
Path("private/key.pem").write_text("secret\n")
os.symlink(os.path.abspath("private"), "srv/uploads/ada/keys")

render checks Under lexically, so it accepts a path through the link. check also resolves symlinks, and rejects it:

>>> files = (P(root) / "uploads" / user / SubPath("file")).requires(
...     Under(P(root) / "uploads")
... )
>>> files.render(root="srv", user="ada", file="keys/key.pem")
'srv/uploads/ada/keys/key.pem'
>>> files.check(root="srv", user="ada", file="keys/key.pem")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.ContainmentError: 'srv/uploads/ada/keys/key.pem' resolves outside 'srv/uploads' (required: Under('{root}/uploads'))
>>> files.check(root="srv", user="ada", file="cv.pdf")
PosixPath('srv/uploads/ada/cv.pdf')

items.title: Checks are point-in-time
items.text: check describes the filesystem at the moment it runs. It is not atomic with opening the path afterwards: if another process can change the tree, it can replace a checked file with a symlink before the program opens it. Conditions state what a program expects and catch mistakes. They do not stop another process.

items.title: glob's symlink policy
items.text:
Below an expression's literal prefix, glob does not descend into symlinked directories by default, and with kind="file" it does not yield a link:

>>> listing = P(root) / "uploads" / user / Param("name")
>>> [m.path for m in listing.glob(root="srv")]
['srv/uploads/ada/cv.pdf', 'srv/uploads/ada/keys']
>>> [m.path for m in listing.glob(root="srv", kind="file")]
['srv/uploads/ada/cv.pdf']

The policy decides which directories the walk lists and how it classifies links. It does not make a yielded path safe to open: an entry can be replaced between the walk and the open, as it can between a check and an open.

items.title: Polars
items.text:
wend.frame.resolve_frame renders one expression for every row of a Polars DataFrame whose columns are named after the expression's parameters. It checks every row with the same rules as render, then builds the paths with Polars' own string operations. This page needs Python 3.14 and the polars extra:

pip install "wend[polars]"

resolve_frame is one way to render many paths. A compiled renderer's many method renders any expression from rows of bindings, without Polars (Datasets and shards). The examples build on each other: run them in order.

items.title: Render a column of paths
items.text:
import polars as pl

from wend import Param, Segment, counter
from wend.frame import resolve_frame

root = Param("root")
split = Segment("split", choices={"train", "test"})
filename = counter("shard", width=5, of_total=True, sep="-", suffix=".parquet")
shard = root / split / filename

frame = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "root": ["data", "data", "/mnt/data", "/mnt/data"],
        "split": ["train", "train", "test", "test"],
        "idx": [0, 1, 0, 1],
        "total": [2, 2, 2, 2],
    }
)

resolve_frame returns a String Series named path, with one path per row:

>>> paths = resolve_frame(shard, frame)
>>> paths.name, paths.dtype
('path', String)
>>> for path in paths:
...     print(path)
data/train/shard-00000-of-00002.parquet
data/train/shard-00001-of-00002.parquet
/mnt/data/test/shard-00000-of-00002.parquet
/mnt/data/test/shard-00001-of-00002.parquet

Each path is the one render returns for that row:

>>> paths.to_list() == [shard.render(row) for row in frame.iter_rows(named=True)]
True
>>> frame.with_columns(path=paths).columns
['root', 'split', 'idx', 'total', 'path']

A LazyFrame is accepted too. The result is collected.

items.title: Path columns are normalised
items.text:
A column at a path position, such as root here, is normalised as render normalises a path: data/, ./data and /mnt//data become data, data and /mnt/data. A column whose values are all normalised already skips that work.

>>> messy = frame.with_columns(
...     pl.Series("root", ["data/", "./data", "/mnt//data", "/mnt/./data"])
... )
>>> resolve_frame(shard, messy).to_list() == paths.to_list()
True

items.title: Missing columns take defaults
items.text:
A parameter with no column takes its default on every row, as render does for a missing binding:

>>> total = Param("total", type=int, default=2)
>>> sized_filename = counter(
...     "shard", width=5, of_total=True, sep="-", suffix=".parquet", total=total
... )
>>> sized = root / split / sized_filename
>>> resolve_frame(sized, frame.drop("total")).to_list() == paths.to_list()
True

items.title: Every row is checked
items.text:
A value that render rejects raises the same exception class, with the number of the first row that fails. No paths are returned:

>>> bad = frame.with_columns(pl.Series("split", ["train", "val", "test", "test"]))
>>> resolve_frame(shard, bad)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.InvalidBindingError: Row 1: split not in choices
>>> shard.render(root="data", split="val", idx=1, total=2)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.InvalidBindingError: split='val': not one of {'test', 'train'}

A null is always rejected, also where render would format None as text:

>>> from wend import P, T
>>> name = Param("name")
>>> note = P("notes") / T(t"note_{name}.txt")
>>> note.render(name=None)
'notes/note_None.txt'
>>> resolve_frame(note, pl.DataFrame({"name": ["a", None]}))
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
wend.errors.InvalidBindingError: Row 1: name is null

items.title: What it refuses
items.text:
A lowering to Polars exists only where Polars reproduces render exactly. For anything else, resolve_frame raises NotImplementedError, which names the construct. Float columns are refused:

>>> score = Param("score")
>>> checkpoint = root / T(t"model-{score:.3f}.pt")
>>> scores = pl.DataFrame({"root": ["runs", "runs"], "score": [0.91234, 0.8]})
>>> resolve_frame(checkpoint, scores)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
NotImplementedError: Column 'score' of type Float64 cannot be lowered to Polars exactly; use expr.compile().many(rows)

So is !r on a string, which renders the value's repr:

>>> quoted = root / T(t"{name!r}.txt")
>>> resolve_frame(quoted, pl.DataFrame({"root": ["out"], "name": ["a"]}))
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
NotImplementedError: {name!r} (!r on a string) cannot be lowered to Polars exactly; use expr.compile().many(rows)

The fallback renders the same rows with the compiled renderer. iter_rows(named=True) gives one mapping per row:

>>> checkpoint.compile().many(scores.iter_rows(named=True))
['runs/model-0.912.pt', 'runs/model-0.800.pt']

The wend.frame docstring lists exactly what is lowered and what is refused. In outline:

  • Lowered: String, integer and Boolean columns; integer format specs in bases d, b, o, x and X, with fill, alignment, sign, #, 0, width and grouping; string specs with fill, alignment, width and precision; and parent, with_name, with_stem, with_suffix and joins applied to unbound paths.
  • Refused: floats and other column types; !r and !a on strings; format specs that contain a parameter; relative_to on unbound paths; and a declared type= that a column's values are not instances of.

to_polars returns the Polars expression itself, for use inside a larger query. It does not validate: rows that render would reject get unspecified values.

  • Parameters: the checks every row goes through.
  • API reference: wend.frame, resolve_frame, to_polars, PathExpr.compile.

items.title: Pydantic
items.text:
wend.pydantic validates the path fields of a Pydantic model against an expression. A field accepts either a path, which must match the expression, or the bindings to render one. This page needs Python 3.14 and the pydantic extra:

pip install "wend[pydantic]"

The examples build on each other: run them in order, in an empty directory.

items.title: A model with path fields
items.text:
A job reads one day's raw file, writes one shard, and reads a configuration file. Create the files it reads:

from pathlib import Path

Path("data/raw").mkdir(parents=True)
Path("data/raw/mon.csv").write_text("id,value\n1,3\n")
Path("job.toml").write_text("workers = 4\n")

Declare the layouts, then annotate each field with PathOf and the expression it must fit:

from typing import Annotated

from pydantic import BaseModel

from wend import Exists, File, Match, P, Param, Segment, T, counter
from wend.pydantic import PathOf

root, day = Param("root"), Param("day")
split = Segment("split", choices={"train", "test"})

raw = P(root) / "raw" / T(t"{day}.csv")
shard = P(root) / split / counter("shard", width=3, suffix=".parquet")


class Job(BaseModel):
    src: Annotated[Path, PathOf(raw.requires(File, Exists))]
    dst: Annotated[Match, PathOf(shard)]
    config: Annotated[Path, File, Exists]
  • src must match raw, and then be an existing file, because the expression requires File and Exists.
  • dst must match shard. Its type is Match, so the validated value is the path together with its bindings.
  • config has no layout. The conditions File and Exists are validators on their own.

items.title: A path as input
items.text:
>>> job = Job(src="data/raw/mon.csv", dst="data/test/shard_007.parquet", config="job.toml")
>>> job.src
PosixPath('data/raw/mon.csv')
>>> job.dst
Match('data/test/shard_007.parquet', {'root': 'data', 'split': 'test', 'idx': 7})
>>> job.dst["idx"]
7

A path given as input must have exactly one reading by the expression. After it matches, the expression's preconditions (its requires) are checked against the filesystem with the bindings read from the path.

items.title: Bindings as input
items.text:
Anything that is not a path is taken as bindings: a mapping, or an object such as another model or a dataclass (wend.bindings). The path is rendered through the expression when the model is validated, and defaults apply as they do in render:

>>> job = Job(
...     src={"root": "data", "day": "mon"},
...     dst={"root": "data", "split": "train", "idx": 3},
...     config="job.toml",
... )
>>> job.src
PosixPath('data/raw/mon.csv')
>>> job.dst
Match('data/train/shard_003.parquet', {'root': 'data', 'split': 'train', 'idx': 3})

items.title: The field's type
items.text:
The field's type decides the validated value: Path (or another PurePath class), str, or Match. In JSON every one of them is the path string, and the JSON schema records the expression's pattern:

>>> job.model_dump_json()
'{"src":"data/raw/mon.csv","dst":"data/train/shard_003.parquet","config":"job.toml"}'
>>> Job.model_json_schema()["properties"]["dst"]
{'format': 'path', 'title': 'Dst', 'type': 'string', 'x-wend-pattern': '{root}/{split}/shard_{idx:03d}.parquet'}

items.title: Conditions as validators
items.text:
wend's conditions validate a path field without PathOf, and without importing wend.pydantic: Annotated[Path, File, Exists] accepts what Pydantic's FilePath accepts. Under works with a base that has no parameters:

>>> from wend import Under
>>> class Export(BaseModel):
...     out: Annotated[Path, Under(P("/data/exports"))]
>>> Export(out="/data/exports/2026-10")
Export(out=PosixPath('/data/exports/2026-10'))

A base with parameters needs bindings, so it is declared on an expression, and the field is annotated with PathOf(expr). Annotating the field with it directly raises TypeError when the class is defined:

>>> class Upload(BaseModel):
...     path: Annotated[Path, Under(P(root))]
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
TypeError: Under('{root}') needs bindings for ['root']: declare it on an expression and annotate the field with PathOf(expr)

items.title: Invalid input
items.text:
Invalid input raises a Pydantic ValidationError, with one error for each field that fails. The error type says what failed: wend_no_match, wend_ambiguous, wend_render (bindings that do not render) or wend_condition.

>>> from pydantic import ValidationError
>>> try:
...     Job(src="data/raw/tue.csv", dst="data/val/shard_001.parquet", config="data")
... except ValidationError as e:
...     print(e)
3 validation errors for Job
src
  'data/raw/tue.csv' does not exist (required: Exists) [type=wend_condition, input_value='data/raw/tue.csv', input_type=str]
dst
  data/val/shard_001.parquet does not match {root}/{split}/shard_{idx:03d}.parquet [type=wend_no_match, input_value='data/val/shard_001.parquet', input_type=str]
config
  'data' is not a regular file (required: File) [type=wend_condition, input_value='data', input_type=str]

Bindings that do not render report the same error as render:

>>> try:
...     Job(
...         src="data/raw/mon.csv",
...         dst={"root": "data", "split": "train"},
...         config="job.toml",
...     )
... except ValidationError as e:
...     print(e.errors()[0]["type"], e.errors()[0]["msg"])
wend_render Missing bindings: ['idx']

A path that the expression reads in more than one way is rejected, and the message lists the readings:

>>> stem, ext = Param("stem"), Param("ext")
>>> class Package(BaseModel):
...     file: Annotated[str, PathOf(P("dist") / T(t"{stem}.{ext}"))]
>>> try:
...     Package(file="dist/tool-1.0.tar.gz")
... except ValidationError as e:
...     print(e.errors()[0]["type"])
wend_ambiguous

Checking conditions reads the filesystem, so validating a model with conditions is an effect. The checks describe the filesystem at the moment of validation (Effects).

items.title: The repository
items.text: path holds src/wend/ the package. Public modules (wend, wend.fs, wend.infer, wend.schema, ...) re-export from private ones (_expr.py, _match.py, _fs.py, ...) tests/ the tests, one file per area, named *_test.py examples/ runnable scripts, each run by tests/examples_test.py bench/bench.py the benchmarks docs/SEMANTICS.md the contract: what every operation must compute docs/MIGRATING.md the changes from 0.1 docs/journal/ the development journal (Project history) docs/site/, zensical.toml this site (Documentation)

items.title: Setting up
items.text:
wend needs Python 3.14 or later. uv installs the package with its test dependency group, which is the default group:

uv sync
uv run pytest

just test runs the same tests with the project's Python. The test group includes the optional integrations (Pydantic, fsspec, Polars), so their tests run too.

The hooks in .pre-commit-config.yaml (ruff, ruff format, file checks and a conventional-commit check on the message) run with prek or pre-commit:

prek install
just pc-fix        # run every hook on every file

CI runs the tests on every CPython version from 3.14 that uv provides, including pre-releases.

items.title: The contract and its tests
items.text:
docs/SEMANTICS.md states what wend computes, independently of how. Two kinds of test check the code against it:

  • tests/contract_test.py holds a reference evaluator written from the contract alone. It evaluates terms strictly with pathlib and imports only wend's parameter declarations, never its expressions, matcher or compiler. Hypothesis generates random terms and checks that wend agrees with it.
  • tests/oracle_test.py builds each random expression twice, once with wend and once as the eager pathlib computation on the formatted strings. If wend renders a value, the oracle renders the same one; if the oracle raises, so does wend.

A change to the contract comes with the matching change to the reference evaluator, in the same pull request, and the reverse. SEMANTICS.md §8 says which guarantees hold by construction and which are only tested.

items.title: Benchmarks
items.text:
uv run python bench/bench.py --quick
uv run python bench/bench.py matching discovery

Each timing is the median of several repeats, in nanoseconds per item, next to baselines such as eager pathlib joins and hand-written regular expressions. Absolute numbers depend on the machine, so compare rows within one run.

items.title: Conventions
items.text:
• Commits follow Conventional Commits (feat(union): ..., fix(core): ..., docs: ...), checked by a commit-message hook. just commit "message" runs the fixers first and stages what they change.
  • Journal entries. A piece of work with decisions worth keeping gets an entry in docs/journal/, named YYYY-MM-DD-topic-<number>.md after its issue or pull request, in the format of docs/JOURNAL.md.
  • Documentation. A change to public behaviour updates the README, SEMANTICS.md where the contract changes, and the pages of this site that describe it. Their examples are tests, so a stale example fails CI.

items.title: Documentation
items.text: The site is built with Zensical from zensical.toml and the Markdown pages in docs/site/. docs/SEMANTICS.md, docs/MIGRATING.md and the journal in docs/journal/ stay where they are, and the site links to them.

items.title: Building locally
items.text:
just docs-serve   # build, serve on http://localhost:8000/wend/, rebuild on change
just docs-build   # a clean, strict build into site/
just docs-check   # the build, then check_site.py and the examples

The toolchain is pinned in .just/docs.just and in .github/workflows/site.yml; change both together. It is not part of the project's dependencies.

items.title: The API reference
items.text:
The pages in docs/site/reference/api/ are generated by mkdocstrings from the source in src/wend/, by static analysis with griffe. Building the reference does not import wend or its optional dependencies.

  • filters = "public" follows each module's __all__, and names without a leading underscore where a module has none.
  • Docstrings are Markdown in the Google style: Args:, Returns:, Raises: and Examples: sections. Link to another object with [name][wend.Name].
  • docs/scripts/griffe_wend.py removes special methods that only implement object protocols (__repr__, __eq__, ...), and works around a griffe bug with nested t-strings.

items.title: Checks
items.text:
--strict fails the build on a broken link, anchor or cross-reference. griffe's docstring warnings do not fail it, so the workflow fails on any line of the build log that starts with griffe:. Then docs/scripts/check_site.py checks that:

  • every Markdown page under docs/site/ is in the nav, and every nav entry exists;
  • every internal link and anchor in the built site resolves;
  • every page is listed in the llmstxt sections of zensical.toml, with the same description as its front matter, and has a Markdown copy;
  • every name in each public module's __all__ has an entry in the API reference.

items.title: Examples are tests
items.text: uv run pytest docs runs the code on every page: each page is one test, and its python and pycon blocks run in order in one namespace, in a fresh temporary working directory. A pycon block is a doctest, so its output must match. A block whose info string contains notest is skipped. A fenced block inside an HTML comment runs but is not shown, which suits setup such as creating the files an example reads.

items.title: Agents and llms.txt
items.text: The llmstxt plugin writes llms.txt (an index of the pages, with their descriptions), llms-full.txt (every listed page, including the API reference, as Markdown) and a Markdown copy of each page at <page>/index.md, linked from the page's head. Each page also has a "Copy as Markdown" action.

items.title: Publishing
items.text:
.github/workflows/site.yml builds the site on every pull request that touches it and on every push to master.

  • Production: a push to master publishes to the root of the gh-pages branch, which GitHub Pages serves at https://lmmx.github.io/wend/.
  • Previews: a pull request from this repository gets a preview at https://lmmx.github.io/wend/pr-preview/pr-<number>/, linked from a comment on the pull request. It is updated on every push and removed when the pull request closes. Previews are deployed only once Pages serves the gh-pages branch.

items.title: Releasing
items.text: A release bumps the version in pyproject.toml, commits and tags it, and publishes the built package to PyPI.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. Run the "Deploy Release" workflow (.github/workflows/deploy.yml) from the repository's Actions tab. It runs just release on master, which:
  2. bumps the patch version with uv version --bump patch;
  3. commits it as chore(release): bump 🐍 -> v<version>;
  4. tags the commit with the version;
  5. pushes the commit and the tag.
  6. CI publishes it (.github/workflows/CI.yml). It builds the wheel and the sdist, generates artifact attestations, and publishes to PyPI with Trusted Publishing, so no token is stored in the repository. A tag pushed by a workflow starts no other workflow, so CI.yml runs when "Deploy Release" completes, or when a tag is pushed from a person's machine.

For a minor or major release, run just release minor (or major) locally on master instead. It does the same steps and pushes from your machine. just release --help shows the options of uv version --bump.

items.title: After a release
items.text:
• The documentation site is published from master on every push, so it already describes the released code.
  • Add the release's changes to docs/MIGRATING.md where they change behaviour.

One page per public module, generated from the docstrings with mkdocstrings. Names starting with _ are left out.

items.title: wend.anchors
items.text:
Anchors: the standard places a path starts from, read from the environment only when asked.

Each anchor is an Absolute parameter named after its environment variable, so an expression built on one stays symbolic, portable and matchable::

from wend import anchors
from wend.anchors import XDG

models = (P("models") / Param("name")).under(XDG.CACHE_HOME / "myapp")
models  # PathExpr('{XDG_CACHE_HOME}/myapp/models/{name}')
models.render(anchors.bindings(), name="bert")  # reads the environment now

render stays pure: nothing here is read until bindings is called, and a test binds the anchors like any parameter (XDG_CACHE_HOME="/tmp/c").

The XDG directories follow the XDG Base Directory specification on every POSIX platform, macOS included: the variable when it is set to an absolute path, otherwise the specification's default below the home directory. For platform conventions instead (~/Library/Caches on macOS), bind the anchor to what a library such as platformdirs reports.

items.text:
CWD: Final = Absolute('CWD')

The process's working directory, os.getcwd() (not $PWD).

items.title: HOME module-attribute
items.text:
HOME: Final = Absolute('HOME')

The user's home directory: $HOME, else the password database.

items.title: XDG
items.text:
XDG()

The XDG base directories (anchors, not values): XDG.CACHE_HOME / "myapp" is {XDG_CACHE_HOME}/myapp.

items.title: CONFIG_HOME class-attribute instance-attribute
items.text:
CONFIG_HOME: Final = Absolute('XDG_CONFIG_HOME')

User configuration: $XDG_CONFIG_HOME, else ~/.config.

User data: $XDG_DATA_HOME, else ~/.local/share.

User caches: $XDG_CACHE_HOME, else ~/.cache.

items.title: bindings
items.text:
bindings(environ: Mapping[str, str] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]

Every anchor's value, read now: an effect, unlike render.

environ defaults to os.environ. A variable that is unset, empty or relative falls back to its default, as the XDG specification requires. CWD is os.getcwd(), and is left out if the working directory no longer exists, so only an expression that uses it fails to render.

items.title: wend.conditions
items.text:
Conditions: what a path must be, and may be used for, when it is realised.

An expression can declare conditions about the filesystem (Exists, Absent), about the kind of thing it names (File, Dir), about how it will be used (Readable, Writable, Creatable, Listable) and about where it may lead (Under(base))::

src = (P(root) / "raw" / T(t"{name}.csv")).requires(File, Exists, Readable)
dst = (P(root) / "out" / T(t"{name}.parquet")).requires(Absent, Creatable)
dst = dst.ensures(File, Exists)

PathExpr.render stays pure: the only condition it enforces is the lexical part of Under, which needs no filesystem. Everything else is checked by an explicit step, PathExpr.check (preconditions) and PathExpr.confirm (postconditions), or by a Step that groups the paths of one pipeline step.

Checks are point in time. A path that exists when it is checked may be gone when it is opened, and a symlink may be swapped between the two: checks describe and catch mistakes, they are not a sandbox and do not prevent races. See docs/SEMANTICS.md §10.

items.title: Absent module-attribute
items.text:
Absent = Condition('Absent')

Nothing occupies the path's name, not even a broken symlink.

items.title: Condition
items.text:
Condition(name: str)

A property of a path, checked when the path is realised.

items.text: name = name

items.text:
__call__(
    path: Any, /, *, optional: bool = False, many: bool = False, open: bool = False
) -> Entry

File(path, ...) and Dir(path, ...) declare a schema entry (see wend.schema): a relative path that names a file or directory, with its cardinality. Other conditions are not callable.

items.text:

The path exists, or could be created now: its nearest existing ancestor is a directory the process may write to and search.

The path names a directory: if it exists it is one.

The path names a regular file: if it exists it is one, and nothing can be joined below it. Add Exists to require that it exists.

items.title: Step
items.text:
Step(paths: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, /, **named: Any)

The paths one step of a pipeline uses, with their conditions.

A single declaration of what must hold before the step runs (each path's requires) and after it finishes (each path's ensures)::

convert = Step(src=src, dst=dst)
with convert(root="/data", name="a") as p:
    write(transform(read(p["src"])), p["dst"])

Entering checks every precondition and yields the rendered paths; leaving without an exception checks every postcondition. The bindings are shared: each path takes the parameters it uses.

Paths declaring none are listed with no verbs. This reports declarations, not behaviour.

base is rendered with the same bindings as the path, so its parameters must be among the path's. Lexically, the path must start with the base's components and have no .. after them.

items.title: wend.errors
items.text:
Exception hierarchy.

Every error raised deliberately by wend derives from WendError. Errors that signal an unacceptable value also derive from ValueError, so callers that already handle pathlib's ValueError keep working. Misused arguments raise TypeError or ValueError, as Python's own functions do; the private helpers at the end hold the argument rules that several entry points share.

Raised when a value would silently change the segment structure of the expression (a separator inside a segment, an empty segment, .), escape upwards (..), or violate a declared type, kind or set of choices.

The filesystem could not say: the path could not be examined (no permission to look, a symlink loop, a failed request), or the backend cannot report the capability without exercising it (whether an object store would accept a write). items.title: wend.frame
items.text:
Vectorised resolution with Polars (optional dependency: pip install wend[polars]).

resolve_frame renders an expression for every row of a DataFrame whose columns are named after the expression's parameters, after validating every row with the same rules as PathExpr.render. to_polars returns the raw pl.Expr (no validation) for embedding in larger queries.

A lowering exists only where Polars reproduces render exactly: for every row, resolve_frame either returns what render returns or raises because render raises (null values are always rejected). Everything else raises NotImplementedError; use expr.compile().many(rows) for those expressions.

items.title: What is lowered
items.text:
Path operands (String columns): Path and absolute heads and SubPath splices, canonicalised exactly as str(PurePosixPath(s)): a/, ./a, a//b and /a/./b are normalised, exactly two leading slashes are kept, three or more become one, and an empty or dot-only relative path is .. Segment parameters from String, integer (str(v)) and Boolean (True/False) columns.

Formatted fields with a static format spec
  • Strings (String columns, !s conversions, nested text, and the name/stem/suffix of a path): [[fill]align][0][width] [.precision][s] with alignment <, > or ^.
  • Integers (Int8 to Int64, UInt8 to UInt64; Int128 and UInt128 in decimal): types d, b, o, x, X or none, with any fill, all four alignments, sign (+, -, space), #, 0, width, and , or _ grouping (zero padding included); !s/!r/!a (all give the decimal digits) followed by a string spec.
  • Booleans: an empty spec (True/False), a non-empty integer spec (Python formats a bool with a spec as 1 or 0), or a conversion followed by a string spec.
Deferred operations on unbound paths

parent, with_name, with_stem, with_suffix, a join with a path parameter, and the name/stem/suffix of such paths.

Refused (NotImplementedError): Float and other column types, and non-String columns at path positions; n, c and float presentation types on integers, and bases other than ten on 128-bit integers; !r/!a on strings; specs that Python rejects for the column's type (a precision on an integer, a sign on a string...); format specs that contain a parameter; relative_to on unbound paths; a declared type= that the column's values are not instances of; and choices= not all of the column's value type.

items.title: to_polars
items.text:
to_polars(expr: PathExpr, schema: Schema | None = None) -> Expr

Lower expr to a Polars expression named path (without validation).

Rows that render accepts get exactly its result; other rows get unspecified values. Pass the frame's schema so integer and Boolean columns are formatted by their type rather than guessed from the expression.

items.title: resolve_frame
items.text:

items.title: wend.fs
items.text:
Filesystems for discovery: the local disk, fsspec, and object stores.

glob and infer read a tree through FileSystem, a small protocol: - list a directory; - say what a path is; - identify a directory, to detect link cycles; - walk a tree; - give a view of one subtree for the duration of one walk.

LocalFS, the default, implements it with os. FsspecFS adapts an fsspec filesystem, so the same expressions discover keys in memory or in S3, GCS or Azure storage. render, match and Lens never touch a filesystem, so they need nothing from here.

Paths stay in the filesystem's own namespace. fsspec strips a URL's protocol: memory://data/x is /data/x and s3://bucket/x is bucket/x. url_to_fs splits a URL into a filesystem and such a path, which is then bound like any root::

fs, root = url_to_fs("s3://bucket/data")
expr.glob(root=root, fs=fs)

A URL is not an expression's head. pathlib reads s3://bucket as the path s3:/bucket, so glob refuses one with a pointer to url_to_fs.

items.text:
FsspecFS(fs: Any, *, listing: Literal['flat', 'tree'] = 'flat')

An fsspec filesystem: object storage (S3, GCS, Azure), memory, HTTP...

listing decides how glob and infer read a tree:

  • "flat" (default): one find for everything below the expression's literal prefix, which glob then walks in memory. On an object store that is a single prefix listing (one request per page of keys) however deep the layout, where a directory-by-directory walk makes one request per directory.
  • "tree": one ls for each directory the expression reaches, as on the local disk. Suited to filesystems with real directories (SFTP, HDFS), where find itself lists every directory, and to prefixes holding many keys that the expression never reaches.

Results are the same either way. Within one walk, a path whose parent has been listed is classified without another request.

Stores have no symlinks: no entry is a link, so glob's symlink options change nothing, and dir_key is None. A directory is a prefix of some key or an explicit marker (a key ending in /, or makedirs on the memory filesystem), so an empty directory exists only as a marker. A key that is also a prefix of other keys is a directory. Keys with an empty, . or .. segment cannot be rendered by any expression and are never listed.

fsspec's own local filesystem is refused: use LocalFS, which keeps glob's symlink policy and cycle detection.

items.title: wend.infer
items.text:
Filesystem layout inference: from observed paths to wend expressions.

The analogue of JSON schema inference (genson, polars-genson) for directory trees. Observed paths form a tree, which is generalised bottom-up:

  • Names are tokenised into ASCII digit runs and the text between them, giving a skeleton (chunk_#-of-#.parquet). A name holding exactly one UUID, or one hex token of eight or more digits mixing letters and digits, keeps that token as one string token, and the text after it stays literal (part-#-<uuid>-c000.snappy.parquet). Siblings with the same skeleton merge; each digit run that varies becomes an int field whose format spec (04d, d) is chosen so that every observed value round-trips, and runs that never vary stay literal. Names whose runs need different specs are split, so a stray epoch_7 among epoch_001... is reported on its own.
  • Sibling directories whose contents are structurally similar (Jaccard similarity of their children's skeletons) collapse into one segment field, like genson's record-to-map unification. Files that share an extension collapse into {stem}.ext once there are min_files of them, and so do empty directories, which have no contents to compare. A map at a position absorbs the similar directories, same-extension files and empty directories beside it, whatever their number.
  • Merging directories re-unifies their children. A field whose observed values always equal an earlier field's becomes the same parameter (n01440764/n01440764_10026.JPEG).

Opaque families. Directories that hold only files, but whose names share no skeleton (terminfo's a/att4410, b/bvt100...), are compared by the extensions of their files instead. Like genson-core's map threshold, this coarser comparison needs many siblings: only a group of at least min_opaque (8) such directories, joining clusters that did not merge by skeleton, collapses into a map, so a code repository's handful of top-level directories stays a record. An empty directory says nothing about extensions: it neither counts towards min_opaque nor keeps a family (0...9 with an empty 9) from being opaque. Inside such an opaque map, a name family seen in only one of its directories is treated like a one-off name, and a {name} map takes in the files left over: their names carry no shared structure.

Variable depth. After flattening, a tail T (one segment, possibly after literal directory segments such as __pycache__, with some literal text) that recurs below a prefix A becomes the layout A/{rel...}/T. Writing holders for the directories that hold an instance of T directly, the recursion criterion is:

  1. T occurs directly in A (depth 0);
  2. T occurs at min_depths (3) distinct depths below A counting depth 0, each depth other than 0 with at least two observed paths;
  3. it branches: at some depth below A there are two or more holders, so T recurs in sibling directories rather than along one chain;
  4. the root looks like what it recurses into: the extensions of the files directly in the depth-0 holders and in the deeper holders are alike (weighted Jaccard of their frequencies at least similarity).

The layouts it replaces are those extending A whose every path ends in an instance of T. Candidates are taken largest first, so the outermost recursion root wins, and a fold below a field segment (site-packages/{pkg}) takes in the folds of literal directories beside it that its field matches. A chain of literal directories fails the third condition (a/{stem}.txt, a/b/{stem}.txt, a/b/c/{stem}.txt); a repository root whose few scripts sit among records (README.md, pyproject.toml) fails the fourth, so its packages fold below it, if at all; and a tail without literal text ({name}) is never a candidate.

Kinds. The observed paths are files and observed directories: the empty directories of a walk, or the entries ending in "/" of an iterable. Each layout has one kind and is inferred from paths of that kind only; a directory merged with others keeps its own observed path apart from the files below it, as a dir layout of the merged pattern ({dir}/examples when some package directories hold an empty examples/). A dir layout generalises like a file layout, through merged parents, digit runs, maps and SubPath folds, but a file and a directory never share one, whatever names they share.

Every observed path matches at least one inferred layout of its kind, and each layout's count and field statistics come from the paths it was inferred from, so the counts partition the observed paths of each kind. optional and cardinality are properties of the pattern and the kind: a layout's paths are the observed paths of its kind that it matches; it is optional when some observed directory matching a proper prefix of it contains none of them, and many when some directory holds more than one of them directly (every such directory matches the pattern's parent prefix). Statistics record the values seen without constraining new ones.

Field names follow the text before a run (epoch_{epoch:03d}), dates ({year:04d}-{month:02d}-{day:02d}, {date:08d}, a bare four-digit {year:04d} directory, and times after a date) and token kinds ({uuid}, {hex}); a directory field is named after its parent.

items.title: wend.lineage
items.text:
Lineage: where a path came from, before and after it exists (SEMANTICS.md §13).

A path has two pasts.

  • As a plan, an expression records how it was built (§9): upstream lists the expressions it derives from, explain writes the chain out, and tags collects the tags (e.tag(source="upload")) found along it.
  • As an artefact, a file was produced from other files by some operation. A Ledger records that, with the inputs' content digests, so later you can ask what a file was made from (provenance, upstream), what was made from it (downstream) and whether it is out of date (stale). Ledger.run records a Step automatically.

Content addressing names a path after what it holds: content_key(*paths) digests files (an effect), values_key(**values) digests plain values (pure), and either is bound to an ordinary parameter, so render stays pure and match reads the key back::

cache = P(root) / "cache" / T(t"{key}") / "features.parquet"
out = cache.render(root="/data", key=content_key(raw))
cache.match(out)["key"] == content_key(raw)   # still true while raw is unchanged

wend records relations; scheduling (what to rebuild, in which order) is left to the caller or a workflow tool.

Pydantic integration (optional dependency: pip install 'wend[pydantic]').

Two kinds of field metadata, for typing.Annotated:

  • PathOf(expr): the field holds a path of expr's layout. A path given as input must match expr; bindings given as input (a mapping, or an object such as another model) are rendered through it, which resolves the path at validation time, as Pydantic's ImportString imports. Either way, expr's preconditions (requires) are then checked against the filesystem::

    class Job(BaseModel): shard: Annotated[Path, PathOf(shard.requires(File, Exists))] last: Annotated[Match, PathOf(shard)] # the path and its bindings

  • wend's conditions themselves (File, Dir, Exists, Absent, Readable, Writable, Creatable, Listable, and Under with a static base) validate a path field: Annotated[Path, File, Exists] is Pydantic's FilePath. They work without importing this module, which they load when Pydantic asks for their schema.

The field's type decides the validated value: Path (or another PurePath class), str, or Match for the path with its bindings. In JSON, every one of them is the path string.

Checks touch the filesystem when the model is validated, and describe it at that moment (docs/SEMANTICS.md §10): validation is an effect here.

Queries: discovery plans that filter what a pattern finds (SEMANTICS.md §11).

A query starts from an expression or a union and adds filters::

src = P("src") / SubPath("rel") / T(t"{stem}.py")
tests = P("src") / SubPath("rel") / T(t"{stem}_test.py")
recent = (src - tests).where(File, modified_after(yesterday))
for m in recent.glob():
    ...
  • q - pattern drops paths that pattern matches;
  • q & pattern keeps paths that pattern also matches, adding its bindings (a parameter both patterns bind must agree);
  • q.where(*predicates) keeps paths for which every predicate holds. A predicate is a condition (File, Readable, Under(base)...), a filesystem test such as modified_after, or any callable taking the Match.

Nothing runs until glob (or match) is called, and results stream as they are found. Filters are a conjunction: wend runs the pattern filters first, then pure callables, then the predicates that touch the filesystem, which is the cheapest order and gives the same results.

items.title: wend.schema
items.text:
Directory schemas: declare a project's layout once, then bind, validate and scaffold it.

A schema is a class whose attributes are entries, each a relative path (a string, t-string or expression) that names a file or a directory::

from wend import Dir, File, Param, T
from wend.schema import Tree

index = Param("index", type=int)

class MLProject(Tree):
    data = Dir("data")
    raw = Dir(data / "raw")
    processed = Dir(data / "processed")
    models = Dir("models")
    checkpoints = File(models / T(t"model-{index:03d}.pt"), many=True)
    config = File("config.yaml")

project = MLProject("/srv/project")
project.config            # PathExpr('/srv/project/config.yaml', requires=(File, Exists))
project.validate()        # a Report: missing, extra, misfiled, wrong-kind ... paths
project.scaffold()        # creates the directories (an explicit effect)

An entry's cardinality says how many paths matching it each directory that matches its parent holds: exactly one by default, optional=True for at most one, many=True for any number, both for "zero or more". from_inferred turns an inferred wend.infer.Schema into a schema class, and Tree.source prints a schema as Python, so a layout can be inferred from a tree, reviewed, edited and kept as code. See docs/SEMANTICS.md §12.

items.title: wend.templates
items.text:
Readymade templates: counter filename patterns.

Part 3 of Future Paths observes that sized and unsized counters are the same few t-strings written again and again. counter writes them once::

counter("log", width=5, suffix=".parquet")
# PathExpr('log_{idx:05d}.parquet')
counter("chunk", width=3, of_total=True, suffix=".parquet")
# PathExpr('chunk_{idx:03d}-of-{total:03d}.parquet')

A counter is an ordinary one-segment expression: join it below a directory, render it, match it, glob it. Its parameters are integers formatted with d, so matching parses them back as int, and a literal after each field that does not start with a digit keeps matching on its single-parse fast path.

items.title: counter
items.text:
counter(
    stem: str = "",
    *,
    width: int | None = None,
    suffix: str = "",
    of_total: bool = False,
    sep: str = "_",
    of: str = "-of-",
    idx: str | Param = "idx",
    total: str | Param = "total",
) -> PathExpr

A counter filename: {stem}{sep}{idx}{suffix}, or, with of_total, {stem}{sep}{idx}{of}{total}{suffix} (a sized counter, which says how many there are).

width zero-pads every number to that many digits ({idx:04d}); without it they are unpadded ({idx:d}). sep is only written when there is a stem. idx and total name the parameters, or are Params to use (declared type=int by default), so a declared default carries over: counter("chunk", of_total=True, total=Param("total", type=int, default=10)).

items.title: wend
items.text:
Symbolic, typed, invertible filesystem paths built from Python t-strings.

A path expression records how a path is built (which parts are literal, which are parameters, how values are formatted) instead of collapsing it to a string. The same expression can be resolved with bindings, partially bound, transformed structurally, matched against concrete paths, used to discover files on disk, and compiled for fast batch resolution.

Target parameters that the source does not provide are bound per call, by keyword or after the path, in a mapping or an object whose fields bind by name (see wend.bindings): lens(path, run="r1"), lens(path, {"run": "r1"}) or lens(path, job). The path is positional-only, so a parameter may have any name.

map(

Pairs (path, mapped), in order, for each path that matches the source; other paths are skipped.

mapping and keyword arguments bind target parameters, as for render. A target parameter named ambiguous is bound through mapping; as a keyword it raises TypeError (see wend.glob).

ambiguous decides what happens to a path that cannot be mapped uniquely: one that matches the source more than one way, or, through a lossless lens, one whose target reads back more than one way (another source path would map to the same target). "raise" (default) raises AmbiguousMatchError when that path is reached; "skip" leaves it out; a callable is called with the AmbiguousMatchError and the path is left out, so ambiguous=report.append collects them. The error names the path that reads more than one way (the source path, or the target path for a collision) and every verified reading of it. As with wend.glob, a callback keeps map an iterator of pairs.

items.title: wend.glob
items.text:
glob(
    expr: PathExpr,
    mapping: Any = None,
    /,
    *,
    kind: str | None = None,
    follow_symlinks: bool = False,
    recurse_symlinks: bool = False,
    ambiguous: Literal["raise", "skip"]
    | Callable[[AmbiguousMatchError], object] = "raise",
    fs: FileSystem | None = None,
    **kw: Any,
) -> Iterator[Match]

Yield a Match for every existing path that expr can render.

Bindings in mapping and keyword bindings fix parameters before the walk (the head of the expression must be bound or literal). kind restricts results to "file" or "dir". Matches are yielded in path order. Argument errors are raised by the call; the walk runs as the result is iterated.

Options and bindings. Options are keyword-only. A parameter that shares an option's name (kind, say) is bound through mapping: glob(e, {"kind": "raw"}, kind="file") binds the parameter and sets the option. A kind= keyword without "kind" in mapping could mean either, so it raises TypeError. To set the option and leave such a parameter free, rename the parameter first: e.bind(kind=Param("k")).

Ambiguity. A path that the expression renders under more than one binding has no single Match. ambiguous decides what happens to it:

  • "raise" (default): raise AmbiguousMatchError for the first such path, before any match is yielded;
  • "skip": leave it out and yield the other matches;
  • a callable: call it with an AmbiguousMatchError for each such path, then yield the other matches. ambiguous=report.append collects them; a callable that raises aborts the walk, as "raise" does.

An ambiguous path is never yielded. Its error carries the path and all its readings, each a verified binding of expr (given bindings included) that renders to the path. A path reached through a followed symlink is also checked with match_all, so a reading that the link policy kept the walk from still counts. Errors are reported in path order, before the first match is yielded.

A callback rather than a returned report object keeps glob an iterator of matches, makes "raise" the special case of a callback that raises (as with os.walk's onerror), and means a report is never read before the walk has filled it.

Symlinks. The walk starts at the expression's fixed prefix (its head and the literal segments that follow it), which is resolved like any path. Below that, symlinks are not followed by default: a symlinked directory is not descended into at any position, and kind judges a link as itself (neither a file nor a directory), so a link can only be yielded as the final component with kind=None. follow_symlinks=True descends symlinked directories at segment positions and classifies links by their targets, as pathlib's glob does. recurse_symlinks=True descends them while recursing through a SubPath, skipping any directory already on the current path so that link cycles terminate.

A SubPath can be empty, so where only SubPath parameters follow a position, a path can end there on a file (or a link, under the rules above) as well as on a directory: P("srv") / SubPath("rest") yields the files below srv as well as its directories, as pathlib's srv.glob("**") with files does.

This is a traversal policy, not a sandbox. The fixed prefix is resolved normally, a yielded link points wherever it points, and the tree can change between the walk and any use of its results. Where that matters, open results with O_NOFOLLOW or resolve and check them.

Filesystems. fs is the wend.fs.FileSystem to walk: the local disk by default, or a wend.fs.FsspecFS for an fsspec filesystem such as an object store, where results are the same as for an identical local tree. Paths are in that filesystem's namespace: bind the root that wend.fs.url_to_fs gives (bucket/data for s3://bucket/data). A URL bound as a path is refused. Stores have no symlinks, so the symlink options change nothing there.
